apparatus.la: *Cfr. Arist., Eth. Nic. I, c. 1–7; Magn. Moral. I, c. 3; et Top. III, c. 1, ubi haec divisio diversimode insinuatur.*
apparatus.en: Cf. Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* I, chs. 1–7; *Magna Moralia* I, ch. 3; and *Topics* III, ch. 1, where this division is indicated in various ways.

apparatus.la: *Cod. A cum ed. 1 satis bene adiungit* ad. *Mox Vat., obnitentibus antiquioribus mss. et ed. 4, post* unum *omittit* increatum.
apparatus.en: Cod. A with ed. 1 quite appropriately adds *ad* ("to"). A little further on, Vat. — against the older mss. and ed. 4 — omits *increatum* ("uncreated") after *unum* ("one").

apparatus.la: *Quaest. 30:* Honestum dicitur quod propter se ipsum expetendum est, utile autem quod ad aliud aliquid referendum est. *— Mox ex multis codd. ut A F G H I K T U V aa bb ee ff cum ed. 1 posuimus* vel *pro* et. *Paulo infra Vat. ante* honestum *praemittit* quid, *quod tamen melius cum mss. et edd. 1, 2, 3 omittitur, quia Deus est ipsum honestum per essentiam.*
apparatus.en: Question 30: "*The honorable* is what is to be sought for its own sake, but *the useful* is what is to be referred to something else." — A little later, with many codices (A, F, G, H, I, K, T, U, V, aa, bb, ee, ff) and ed. 1, we have read *vel* ("or") in place of *et* ("and"). A little further on, Vat. prefixes *quid* ("what") before *honestum*, but it is better omitted (with the mss. and edd. 1, 2, 3), since God is the honorable by essence.

apparatus.la: *Quaest. 30:* Omnis itaque humana perversio est, quod etiam vitium vocatur, fruendis uti velle atque utendis frui.
apparatus.en: Question 30: "All human perversity — which is also called vice — is to want to use things that are to be enjoyed, and to enjoy things that are to be used."

apparatus.la: *In Evang. S. Lucae c. 15, ubi iuxta ed. Venet. 1748:* At vero filius, qui habet Spiritus S. pignus in corde, saecularis mercedis lucella non quaerit, quibus serviat. Haeredes sunt etiam mercenarii, qui ducuntur ad vineam. Bonus mercenarius Petrus etc. *— Codex autem, sub n. 507 Bibliothecae Laurentianae Florentiis, membr. in fol. saec. XI, fol. 116 recto, col. 2, ultimam partem sic exhibet:* non quaerit, qui ius servat haeredis. Sunt etiam qui conducuntur ad vineam. Bonus etc. *Cum quo concordat cod. in Plut. XIV. in fol. saec. XV, libr. VII, c. 35. Lectio istius ed. in verbis et interpunctione errat.*
apparatus.en: *Commentary on the Gospel of Luke*, ch. 15, where according to the Venice edition of 1748 [it reads]: "But the son, who has the pledge of the Holy Spirit in his heart, does not seek the paltry pay of a secular reward for those whom he serves. Even heirs are hirelings, who are led to the vineyard. Peter is a good hireling," etc. — Codex 507 of the Laurentian Library in Florence (parchment, fol., 11th cent., fol. 116 recto, col. 2) gives the last part thus: "does not seek [what is of] him who preserves the right of an heir. There are also those who are hired for the vineyard. A good [hireling]," etc.; with which the codex in Plut. XIV (fol., 15th cent., bk. VII, ch. 35) agrees. The reading of that edition errs in both words and punctuation.

apparatus.la: *Vat. contra mss. et ed. 1, invertendo comparationem, nempe* sicut summa bonitas, sic summa veritas, *argumentationem, uti ex subnexis patet, perturbat. Mox cod. X post* clarius *satis bene addit* veritate increata. *Dein, faventibus antiquioribus mss. et ed. 1, expunximus* aliquam, *quod Vat. cum recentiori cod. cc praemittit voci* aliam. *In ultima propositione huius argumenti multi codd. C F G K L R S U V W aa bb cum ed. 1 ante* diligi *falso repetunt* plus.
apparatus.en: Vat., against the mss. and ed. 1, inverts the comparison — reading *sicut summa bonitas, sic summa veritas* — and thereby disturbs the argument, as what follows makes clear. A little later, cod. X after *clarius* ("more clearly") rightly adds *veritate increata* ("than the uncreated truth"). Then, with the older mss. and ed. 1 in our favor, we have struck out *aliquam* ("some"), which Vat. with the later cod. cc prefixes to the word *aliam* ("other"). In the last proposition of this argument, many codices (C, F, G, K, L, R, S, U, V, W, aa, bb) with ed. 1 wrongly repeat *plus* ("more") before *diligi* ("to be loved").

apparatus.la: *Boeth., De diff. topicis II. Locus a fine:* Cuius finis bonus est, ipsum quoque bonum est. *Vide supra q. 1 in corp. Propositio ista derivata esse videtur ex illa Arist., Top. III, c. 1:* Cuius finis melior, et ipsum melius. *Ad normam codd. et ed. 1 omisimus* est *et* quoque, *quod Vat. cum Boethio habet.*
apparatus.en: Boethius, *On Topical Differences* II, near the end: "Whose end is good, the thing itself also is good." See above, q. 1 in body. The proposition seems to derive from Aristotle, *Topics* III, ch. 1: "Whose end is better, is itself also better." On the model of the codices and ed. 1, we have omitted *est* and *quoque* ("is" and "also"), which Vat. — following Boethius — retains.

apparatus.la: *Boeth., De diff. topicis II. — Codd. F O X addunt post* malus *particulam* et. *Immediate post ex fere omnibus mss. et ed. 1 substituimus* quod *loco* quia, *cod. R autem habet* ergo si Deus.
apparatus.en: Boethius, *On Topical Differences* II. — Codd. F, O, X add the particle *et* after *malus* ("evil"). Immediately after, from nearly all the mss. and ed. 1, we have substituted *quod* in place of *quia* ("because"), while cod. R has *ergo si Deus* ("therefore if God").

apparatus.la: *Auctoritate mss. et ed. 1 reiecimus lectionem Vat.* aversionem a fine *tanquam minus rectam, quia talis abusus non dicit solum simplicem aversionem a fine, sed etiam directam perversionem ipsius finis, quatenus nempe ipse finis convertitur in medium. Cod. O post* perversitatem *addit* intentionis. *Cod. R totam propositionem sic exhibet:* et abusus talis semper est mortale peccatum, non (forsan omissum: solum) propter perversitatem in finem cum delectatione, sed propter voluntatis *etc. Mox maiorem partem codd. ut A C G I K L U V X etc. et ed. 1 secuti, bis pro* utimur *substituimus* utitur, *quod grammatice melius est; alii codd. primo loco habent* utitur, *secundo loco* utimur. *Propositio ista relativa a S. Doctore adducta, quae immediate refertur ad substantivum* voluntatis, *continet implicite rationem inordinationis in voluntate hic notatae; sensus enim est: voluntas ordinata minus diligit ipsum quo utitur, i.e. medium, quam propter quod utitur, i.e. finem; atqui in hoc casu habetur contrarium: ergo voluntas est inordinata.*
apparatus.en: On the authority of the mss. and ed. 1, we have rejected Vat.'s reading *aversionem a fine* ("a turning-away from the end") as less correct, because such misuse denotes not merely a simple turning away from the end but also a direct perversion of the end itself, inasmuch as the end itself is turned into a means. Cod. O after *perversitatem* adds *intentionis* ("of intention"). Cod. R gives the whole proposition thus: "and such misuse is always a mortal sin, not (perhaps with *solum*, 'only,' omitted) on account of the perversion into an end with delight, but on account of the will's," etc. A little later, following the greater part of the codices (A, C, G, I, K, L, U, V, X, etc.) and ed. 1, we have twice substituted *utitur* ("he uses") for *utimur* ("we use"), which is grammatically better; other codices have *utitur* in the first place and *utimur* in the second. This relative clause, introduced by the Holy Doctor and referring directly to the substantive *voluntatis* ("of the will"), implicitly contains the reason for the disorder in the will here noted: for the sense is that an ordered will loves that *by which* it uses (i.e., the means) less than that *on account of which* it uses (i.e., the end); but in this case the contrary obtains — therefore the will is disordered.

apparatus.la: *Vers. 1. — Paulo ante exhibemus lectionem codd. R V W X Y Z aa bb; alii codd. autem, omisso* Deus, *ponunt* Dominus *post* Abrahae, *a quibus non multum dissidet Vat. legendo:* est ipse, sicut Dominus dixit ad Abraam. *Mox fide antiquiorum mss. et ed. 1 post* utitur *expunximus* Deo.
apparatus.en: Verse 1. — A little before [this], we give the reading of codd. R, V, W, X, Y, Z, aa, bb; other codices, omitting *Deus*, place *Dominus* ("the Lord") after *Abrahae*, from which Vat. does not differ much, reading: "is himself, as the Lord said to Abram." A little later, on the authority of the older mss. and ed. 1, after *utitur* we have struck out *Deo*.

apparatus.la: *Vat. praeter fidem mss. et ed. 1 hic addit* et sic utitur.
apparatus.en: Vat., against the authority of the mss. and ed. 1, here adds *et sic utitur* ("and so he uses [him]").

apparatus.la: *Vat. post* istum *addit* amorem *et post* illam *adiungit* cognitionem, *quae tamen auctoritate mss. et ed. 1 tanquam superflua expunximus.*
apparatus.en: Vat. after *istum* ("this one," masc.) adds *amorem* ("love"), and after *illam* ("that one," fem.) adds *cognitionem* ("knowledge"), which we have, however, on the authority of the mss. and ed. 1, struck out as superfluous.

apparatus.la: *Cod. cc cum ed. 1* hoc. *Mox antiquiores codd. et ed. 1 omittunt propositionem, quae habetur in Vat. et cod. cc post* ordinatione, *scil.:* et illo modo non contingit uti Deo, quia non convenit ordinari. *— Fusius de hac re tractat S. Doctor II Sent. d. 28 a. 1 q. 1.*
apparatus.en: Cod. cc with ed. 1 reads *hoc* ("this," neut.). A little later, the older codices and ed. 1 omit the sentence found in Vat. and cod. cc after *ordinatione*, namely: "and in that way one cannot use God, since he is not fit to be ordered." — The Holy Doctor treats this matter more fully in II *Sent.* d. 28, a. 1, q. 1.

apparatus.la: *Scilicet:* cuius usus bonus, et ipsum bonum. *— Vat. cum cod. cc paulo ante post* ultimum *praeter fidem antiquiorum mss. et ed. 1 addit* scilicet usus Dei aut est bonus aut malus *etc.*
apparatus.en: Namely: "whose use is good, the thing itself is [good]." — Vat. with cod. cc a little earlier, after *ultimum*, against the authority of the older mss. and ed. 1, adds *scilicet usus Dei aut est bonus aut malus* ("namely, the use of God is either good or evil"), etc.

apparatus.la: *Ex mss. et ed. 1 substituimus* in *loco* ad. *— De hoc secundo responsionis membro vide supra q. 1 circa principium conclusionis.*
apparatus.en: From the mss. and ed. 1 we have substituted *in* ("in") in place of *ad* ("to"). — On this second member of the reply, see above, q. 1, near the beginning of the conclusion. ---

questions.notes:
- **Chunk scope.** This chunk covers Q. III in its entirety, spanning printed pp. 34–35 (PDF pp. 136–137): opening frame, four *videtur quod* arguments, four *Sed contra* arguments, Conclusio, Respondeo, and the four *Ad obiecta* replies. The Scholion block at the foot of p. 35 is included. This closes the first of the three confirmed gaps in d. 1 identified in the rebuild audit. (The legacy raw-OCR range noted in the audit, ~13962–14104, was an under-count: the full chunk runs to ~14175 in `raw/bonaventure_vol1_raw.txt`, with its footnote block continuing through line 14253.)

- **Key terms** (per project glossary): *uti* → use; *frui* → enjoy; *abuti* → misuse; *utibile / fruibile* → usable / enjoyable; *honestum* → honorable (Augustine's technical term for what is sought for its own sake); *utile* → useful; *bonum creatum / increatum* → created / uncreated good; *merces* → reward; *mercenarius* → hireling; *intuitus mercedis* → "with an eye to reward"; *causa movens* → moving cause; *ratio inducens* → prompting reason; *ordinare* → to order (to an end); *aversio a fine* → turning-away from the end.

- **The Boethian axiom in the sed contra.** Objections 3 and 4 *contra* both hinge on Boethius's *De differentiis topicis* II: "whose end is good, the thing itself is good" and "whose use is evil, the thing itself is evil." Bonaventure's reply at Ad 3 distinguishes *finis quantum ad substantiam* from *finis quantum ad intentionem finiendi*, confining Boethius's principle to the latter sense, which consists in *recta ordinatio*.

- **"Looking to reward" (*intuitu mercedis*).** The reply at Ad 1 is a classic Franciscan distinction between two kinds of mercenary: one who regards the reward as a *causa movens* (moving cause) — and so is a *malus mercenarius* — and one who regards it as a *ratio inducens* (prompting reason). Only the former turns service into instrumental *use* of God.

- **Footnote 10 (the long Quaracchi note).** This is the longest critical note in the chunk and straddles the foot of p. 34 and the top of p. 35. It defends the editors' reading *perversitatem in finem* against Vat.'s *aversionem a fine* on the theological ground that *abusio* of the uncreated good is not a mere turning-away but a direct reversal in which the end is itself turned into a means; it also harmonizes the grammar (*utitur* vs. *utimur*) across the codices. The English rendering preserves the editorial voice.

- **Vision transcription status.** This is a first-pass vision re-OCR of printed pp. 34–35 (PDF pp. 136–137), reconciled against the legacy `raw/bonaventure_vol1_raw.txt` (lines 13962–14253) for words obscured by ligature or tight point size in the footnote region. Apparatus footnotes were read from the PDF at small point size and should be considered best-effort — in particular, the long footnote 10 straddles the page break and should be verified on a higher-resolution image pass before publication. Several manuscript sigla may still need cross-check against the Quaracchi Vol. I sigla key (forthcoming in `tools/apparatus-sigla.json`).

questions.title: Dist. 1, Art. 2, Q. 1
questions.titleLa: Utrum frui sit actus voluntatis, an aliarum virium
questions.titleEn: Whether enjoyment is an act of the will, or of the other powers
questions.latin:
<!-- page 35 -->

**ARTICULUS II.** *Quid sit* frui.

Habito de *uti* et *utibili*, consequenter quaeritur de *frui* et *fruibili*, et primo, quid sit *frui* per essentiam, utrum scilicet sit actus voluntatis, an aliarum virium.

**QUAESTIO UNICA.** *Utrum* frui *sit actus voluntatis, an aliarum virium.*

Quod sit actus voluntatis, videtur per primam definitionem, quae est: «*Frui* est amore inhaerere alicui rei propter se ipsam»[^1]; sed amor est voluntatis: ergo et *frui* similiter. Si dicas, quod amor sumitur ibi communiter, secundum quod est in qualibet vi respectu sui actus: contra, in omnibus aliis definitionibus idem dicitur. Unde dicitur in sequenti[^2]: «Fruimur cognitis, in quibus voluntas delectata conquiescit». Quietatio enim voluntatis est. Et in alia[^3] similiter: «Frui est cum gaudio uti». Gaudium autem ad voluntatem proprie pertinet.

<!-- page 36 -->

2. Item, ostenditur ratione, quia fruitione delectamur[^4], secundum quod delectabile est differentia boni, cum sit bonum honestum, conferens et delectabile; bonum autem obiectum est voluntatis: ergo *frui* est solius voluntatis.

3. Item, eo fruimur, quo quietamur; sed quietatio respicit rationem finis, «et finis rationem boni»[^5], et «bonum est obiectum voluntatis»: ergo fruitio, quae ordinat ad illud, similiter est voluntatis.

**Sed contra.**

1. Omnis virtus appetit uniri suo obiecto, quo habito delectatur, si cognoscit, et quiescit: ergo motus cum quietatione et delectatione est omnium virium: ergo cum talis sit fruitio, fruitio erit in omnibus viribus, non tantum in voluntate.

2. Item, absentia rei amatae potius contristat amantem quam delectat[^6]; quod enim delectat ipsum, hoc est, quia videt ipsam et habet. Si ergo motus fruitionis est cum delectatione vel est ipsa delectatio: ergo hoc est, quia videt illud in quo est ipsa delectatio; sed visio respicit cognitivam: ergo etc.

3. Item, Augustinus in libro de *Doctrina christiana*[^7]: «Haec est summa merces, ut ipso perfruamur». Sed super illud Psalmi: *Ostendam illi salutare etc.*, dicit Glossa[^8], quod «visio est tota merces»: ergo si fruitio est merces, fruitio est visio per essentiam; sed visio est in cognitiva sive in ratione: ergo etc.

4. Item, fide et spe tendimus in Deum: aut ergo fruendo, aut utendo; sed non utendo, cum Deo non sit utendum: ergo fruendo: ergo fide et spe fruimur; sed fides est habitus rationis cognitivae; sed cuius est habitus, eius est actus: ergo actus fruitionis est actus rationis; similiter videtur de irascibili: ergo etc.

**Conclusio.**

*Frui sumtum essentialiter est actus voluntatis; sumtum dispositive est actus etiam aliarum potentiarum.*

**Respondeo.** Secundum aliquos[^9] *frui* pertinet ad omnes vires; et hoc dicunt, quia omnes vires remunerabuntur. Qui dicunt etiam quod *frui* in gloria erit magis proprie rationis, quia immediatius se habet ad delectationem.

Sed aliter videtur dicendum secundum Augustinum, scilicet quod sit actus ipsius voluntatis. Cum enim tres dentur definitiones de *frui*, omnes dantur penes actum voluntatis, quem tripliciter est considerare. Primo modo *communiter*, prout dicit motum cum delectatione; et sic definit Augustinus[^10]: «Frui est uti cum gaudio». Secundo modo, prout dicit motum cum quietatione; et hoc modo definitur ab Augustino de *Doctrina christiana*: «Frui est amore inhaerere alicui rei propter se ipsam»; et hoc modo accipitur *proprie*. Tertio modo accipitur, prout complectitur utrumque, scilicet quietationem et delectationem; et hoc modo definitur ab Augustino decimo *de Trinitate*: «Frui est quiescere in cognitis, voluntate propter se delectata»; et sic accipitur *propriissime*.

Quia ergo *frui* secundum omnem acceptionem dicit delectationem vel quietem vel utrumque, et omne tale habet rationem boni, et hoc est obiectum voluntatis: ideo loquendo essentialiter, *frui* est actus voluntatis. Sed quia voluntas nec delectatur nec quietatur nisi in eo quod cognoscit (vel per fidem vel per speciem), et in eo quod habet vel per spem vel in re, ideo actus aliarum virium ad hunc disponunt, non tamen sunt ipsum *frui* essentialiter loquendo.

<!-- page 37 -->

Ex hoc patet solutio ad illud quod communiter solet quaeri, quare *frui* non definitur per actum cognitionis, sicut per actum delectationis. Tamen haec quaestio fundatur super falsum: Augustinus enim ponit in notificationem eius quod dicit: «*Frui* est cognitis», non sicut dispositionem, sed sicut dispositum; et sic cognitio est dispositio ad *frui*, non autem *frui* per essentiam.

**Ad 1.** Ad illud quod obiicitur, cum virtus habet delectari et quiescere in suo obiecto: dicendum, quod per Anselmum[^11] voluntas inclinat alias vires et illas movet et regit, et ideo requiritur ad delectationem inclinatio aliarum virium. Unde sicut voluntas non sibi cognoscit, sed regit cognitionem et facit sibi cognoscendo, sic etiam a cognitione et aliis viribus non accipitur fruitio tanquam eis per se conveniens, sed quia voluntas per eas sibi *fruitur*.

**Ad 2.** Ad illud quod obiicitur, quod viator non fruitur, quia videt quod non habet: dicendum, quod *videre* et *habere* requiruntur ad *frui*, similiter et *amare*: ambo enim videt quis vel habet; sed aliter requiritur visio, aliter requiritur amor. Nam visio et habere requiruntur dispositive, amor autem requiritur essentialiter. Et ideo nullum inconveniens est, fruitionem esse actum voluntatis tanquam radicem, licet exigat dispositiones in aliis viribus.

**Ad 3.** Ad illud quod obiicitur, quod fide et spe fruimur: dicendum, quod ista quae inducuntur non sunt proprie de fide et spe, sed per concomitantiam. Voluntas enim per illas habitus tendit in obiectum suum et in eo quiescit; sed ipsum tendere et quiescere est voluntatis, licet per actus cognitivae disponatur.

**Ad 4.** Ad illud quod obiicitur, quod actus fruitionis est actus rationis: dicendum, quod fide et spe tendimus in Deum quantum ad dispositionem, sed quantum ad consummationem actus, hoc est voluntatis. Similiter et de irascibili dicendum est, quod eius actus disponit, non autem consummat fruitionem.
questions.english:
<!-- page 35 -->

**Article 2.** *What* enjoyment *is.*

Having treated of *use* and the *usable*, we next ask about *enjoyment* and the *enjoyable*, and first, what *enjoyment* is in essence — namely, whether it is an act of the will, or of the other powers.

**Sole Question.** *Whether* enjoyment *is an act of the will, or of the other powers.*

That it is an act of the will seems to follow from the first definition, which is: "*To enjoy* is to cling with love to some thing for its own sake"[^1]; but love is of the will; therefore *enjoyment* likewise [is of the will]. If one replies that *love* is here taken in a general sense — as found in every power with respect to its own act —, one may answer: in all the other definitions the same is said. For in the next one it is said[^2]: "We enjoy the things we know, in which the will takes its delighted rest." But rest is of the will. And in another[^3] it is similarly said: "To enjoy is to use with joy"; and joy properly pertains to the will.

<!-- page 36 -->

2. Again, it is shown from reasoning: because we are delighted in enjoyment[^4], and *delightful* is a differentia of the good (since it is the good that is upright, useful, and delightful); but the good is the object of the will: therefore *enjoyment* belongs to the will alone.

3. Again, we enjoy that in which we come to rest; but rest bears upon the character of an end, "and an end upon the character of the good"[^5], and "the good is the object of the will": therefore enjoyment, which orders toward that [end], likewise [belongs to the will].

**On the contrary.**

1. Every power desires to be united with its object, delights in it once possessed (if it knows it), and comes to rest in it: therefore motion-with-rest-and-delight belongs to every power: therefore, since enjoyment is such a motion, enjoyment will be in all [powers], not only in the will.

2. Again, the absence of the beloved thing saddens the lover more than it delights him[^6]; for what delights him is the fact that he sees it and has it. If, then, the motion of enjoyment is accompanied by delight or is the delight itself: this is so because he *sees* that in which the delight consists; but seeing belongs to the cognitive [power]: therefore etc.

3. Again, Augustine in *On Christian Doctrine*[^7]: "This is the highest reward — that we enjoy Him." But on the verse of the Psalm *I will show him my salvation, etc.*, the Gloss says[^8] that "the vision [of God] is the whole reward": therefore if enjoyment is the reward, enjoyment is vision in essence; but vision is in the cognitive [power] or in reason: therefore etc.

4. Again, by faith and by hope we tend toward God: either, then, by enjoying or by using; but not by using, since God is not to be used: therefore by enjoying: therefore we enjoy by faith and hope; but faith is a habit of the cognitive reason; and whose is the habit, his is the act: therefore the act of enjoyment is an act of reason. The same seems to hold for the irascible [appetite]: therefore etc.

**Conclusion.**

*"To enjoy" taken essentially is an act of the will; taken dispositively, it is an act of the other powers as well.*

**Reply.** According to some[^9], *enjoyment* pertains to all the powers; and they say this because all the powers will be rewarded. They also say that *enjoyment* in glory will belong more properly to reason, because reason bears more immediately upon delight.

But it seems rather that we should say with Augustine that it is the act of the will itself. For since three definitions of *enjoyment* are given, all of them are framed in terms of an act of the will, which can be considered in three ways. First, *commonly*, insofar as it expresses motion with delight; and thus Augustine defines it[^10]: "To enjoy is to use with joy." Second, insofar as it expresses motion with rest; and in this way it is defined by Augustine in *On Christian Doctrine*: "To enjoy is to cling with love to some thing for its own sake"; and in this way it is taken *properly*. Third, it is taken insofar as it embraces both — rest and delight — ; and in this way it is defined by Augustine in Book X *On the Trinity*: "To enjoy is to rest in what one knows, the will being delighted for its own sake"; and in this way it is taken *most properly*.

Since, therefore, *enjoyment* in every acceptation expresses delight or rest or both, and every such thing has the character of the good, and this is the object of the will: it follows that, speaking essentially, *enjoyment* is an act of the will. But because the will neither delights nor rests except in what it knows (either by faith or by species), and in what it has (either by hope or in reality), the acts of the other powers *dispose* toward this [act]; they are not, however, enjoyment itself, essentially speaking.

<!-- page 37 -->

From this is clear the reply to what is commonly asked: why *enjoyment* is not defined by the act of cognition as it is by the act of delight. But this question rests on a false premise: Augustine in fact puts cognition into the description of what he says as that *in which* enjoyment takes place — not as its disposition, but as that-which-is-disposed. And so cognition is a disposition to *enjoyment*, not enjoyment itself in essence.

**Reply to 1.** To the objection that every power has delight and rest in its own object: it must be said that, according to Anselm[^11], the will inclines the other powers and moves and governs them, and therefore the inclination of the other powers is required for [the will's] delight. Hence just as the will does not itself know, but governs cognition and causes cognition for itself, so from cognition and the other powers enjoyment is not received as befitting them in themselves — rather, the will *enjoys for itself through* them.

**Reply to 2.** To the objection that the wayfarer does not enjoy, since he sees what he does not yet have: it must be said that *seeing* and *having* are both required for *enjoyment*, as is *loving*. For one who enjoys both sees and has [his object]; but seeing and having are required dispositively, whereas love is required essentially. And so there is nothing unfitting in saying that enjoyment is an act of the will at its root, even though it requires dispositions in the other powers.

**Reply to 3.** To the objection that we enjoy by faith and hope: it must be said that the texts adduced are not properly about faith and hope, but about them *by concomitance*. For the will, through those habits, tends toward its object and rests in it; but the tending and resting themselves belong to the will, even though they are disposed by the acts of the cognitive [power].

**Reply to 4.** To the objection that the act of enjoyment is an act of reason: it must be said that we tend toward God by faith and hope as regards the *disposition* [to the act], but as regards the *consummation* of the act, this belongs to the will. And the same must be said of the irascible [appetite]: its act disposes toward enjoyment but does not consummate it.
questions.latinScholion:
**I.** In solutione principali huius quaestionis, scil. *quod frui sit actus voluntatis*, consentiunt fere omnes scholastici, praesertim inter doctores antiquos. Conveniunt Alex. Hal., Richard., B. Albert. et S. Thom., licet pars illorum — et praecipue S. Thom. — quatenus eiusmodi actum formaliter considerat quasi actus intellectivae nonnihil recedat a S. Doctore. Re vera neuter ipsorum a fundamentali doctrina Augustiniana discedit.

**II.** Alex. Hal., *Summa* p. II, q. 62, m. 1. — S. Thom., hic q. 1, a. 1; *Summa theol.* I–II, q. 11. — B. Albert., hic a. 1 et 2. — Richard., hic a. 2, q. 1. — Petr. a Tar., hic q. 1, a. 1. — Henr. Gand., S. a. 8, q. 1. — Scot., hic q. 2 et *Quodl.*, q. 16. — Durand., hic q. 1. — Dionys. Carth., hic q. 3. — Biel, hic q. 2.

questions.englishScholion:
**I.** In the main resolution of this question — namely *that enjoyment is an act of the will* — nearly all the scholastics agree, especially among the older doctors. Alexander of Hales, Richard of Mediavilla, Albert the Great, and Thomas Aquinas all concur — although some of them, and especially Thomas, in taking the act formally as an act of the intellective part, depart somewhat from the holy Doctor. Still, neither of them really departs from the fundamental Augustinian doctrine.

**II.** Alexander of Hales, *Summa*, pt. II, q. 62, m. 1. — Thomas Aquinas, here q. 1, a. 1; *Summa theologiae* I–II, q. 11. — Albert the Great, here aa. 1–2. — Richard of Mediavilla, here a. 2, q. 1. — Peter of Tarentaise, here q. 1, a. 1. — Henry of Ghent, *Summa* a. 8, q. 1. — Scotus, here q. 2, and *Quodlibet*, q. 16. — Durandus, here q. 1. — Dionysius the Carthusian, here q. 3. — Biel, here q. 2.

---

questions.notes:
- **Chunk scope.** This chunk covers the entire sole question of Art. II on printed pp. 35–37: the Article-II rubric (*Quid sit frui*), the transitional framing, the three *videtur quod* arguments (pp. 35–36), the four *sed contra* arguments (p. 36), the *conclusio*, the *respondeo* with its three acceptations of *frui*, the four *ad*-replies, and the two-part scholion that closes the article on p. 37. Article III (*De fruibili*) opens on p. 38 and is covered in separate chunks.

- **Chunking correction.** The legacy chunk `vol1/legacy/bon-sent-I-d1-a2-q1.md` was truncated: it began mid-article with the first *videtur quod* and never reached the *ad*-replies, and it was interleaved with a spurious fragment from the preceding Q. III *respondeo*. The present rebuild captures the entire question from the Art. II rubric through the closing scholion. Legacy file moved to `vol1/legacy/`.

- **Key terms** (per project glossary): *frui* → enjoy / enjoyment; *fruibile* → enjoyable; *quietatio / quiescere* → rest; *motus cum delectatione* → motion with delight; *dispositive* → dispositively (i.e. as a preparing condition, not as the thing itself); *per concomitantiam* → by concomitance; *essentialiter* → essentially (i.e. in its very essence, as distinct from *dispositive*).

- **Three acceptations of *frui*.** The heart of the *respondeo* is Bonaventure's harmonization of Augustine's three definitions of *frui* — *communiter* (motion with delight; *Qq. 83*, q. 30), *proprie* (motion with rest; *De doctr. christ.*), and *propriissime* (embracing both; *De Trin.* X). The English follows the project glossary in rendering these as *commonly / properly / most properly*, matching q. 1's parallel schema for *uti*.

- **Essentially vs. dispositively.** Bonaventure's central move is to distinguish what enjoyment is *in its root* (an act of the will) from what enjoyment *requires as a disposition* (acts of cognition and of the other powers). The translation tries to keep this distinction visible in every *ad*-reply by preserving the adverbial contrast between *essentialiter* and *dispositive*.

- **Vision transcription status.** First-pass vision re-OCR of printed pp. 35–37 (PDF pp. 137–139). The *respondeo* and *ad*-replies section was cross-checked against the (partial) legacy raw text, which covered roughly through the start of *ad 1*. Apparatus entries remain best-effort first-pass and should be verified on a second vision pass before publication.

questions.titleLa: Utrum Deo sit fruendum
questions.titleEn: Whether God is to be enjoyed
questions.latin:
<!-- page 38 -->

**QUAESTIO I.** *Utrum Deo sit fruendum.*

Circa primum, quod sit Deo fruendum, ostenditur sic.

1. «Eo fruendum est, quod beatos nos facit»[^1], quia in beatitudine est recta fruitio; sed Deo beati efficimur, quia ipse est nostra beatitudo: ergo Deo est fruendum.

2. Item, bonum est amabile; ergo magis bonum magis amabile et summe bonum summe amabile[^2]; sed eo fruimur, quod summe amamus: ergo etc.

3. Item, pulcrum delectat, et[^3] magis pulcrum magis delectat; ergo summe pulcrum summe delectat; sed eo fruimur, in quo summe delectamur: ergo etc.

**Sed contra.**

1. Ubi est fruitio, ibi est delectatio; «sed delectatio est coniunctio convenientis cum convenienti»[^4]; Dei autem ad creaturam nulla est convenientia, immo summa distantia: ergo nec delectatio, ergo nec fruitio.

2. Item, excellens sensibile corrumpit sensum vel saltem contristat, quia delectatio est in mediis[^5]: ergo pari ratione excellens intelligibile corrumpit vel contristat intellectum. Sed Deus est excellentissima lux: ergo contristat, non delectat, ergo etc. Si dicas, quod sensibilis potentia est corruptibilis, non intellectus; hoc non solvit, quia intellectus, dum est in carne, fatigatur et impeditur in actu, corpore corrupto.

3. Item, ubi fruitio, ibi quietatio; sed in infinito non est quietatio, «quia semper est aliquid extra accipere»[^6]: ergo cum Deus sit infinitus, in Deo non est quietatio, ergo nec fruitio.

**Conclusio.**

*Deo proprie est fruendum.*

**Respondeo.** Dicendum, quod Deo fruendum est, eo quod ipse solus perfecte finit[^7] et delectat ipsam animam propter se et super omnia.

**Ad 1.** Ad illud ergo quod obiicitur, quod delectatio est coniunctio convenientis etc.; dicendum, quod[^8] est convenientia per unius naturae participationem vel per comparationem communem. Prima convenientia facit communitatem univocationis, secunda communitatem analogiae sive proportionis. Et haec est secundum triplicem differentiam: aut secundum similem comparationem duorum ad duo, ut sicut homo[^9] ad animal, ita albedo se habet ad colorem; aut secundum dissimilem comparationem duorum ad unum, ut animalis et cibi ad sanitatem; vel

<!-- page 39 -->

secundum comparationem duorum ad invicem, ut puta cum unum est imitatio vel similitudo alterius. Similitudo enim non convenit cum consimili[^10] in tertio, sed se ipsa. Sic est in proposito, quia anima est expressa similitudo Dei. Haec convenientia in uno extremo ponit inclinationem et indigentiam, in alio quietationem et sufficientiam, quia unum[^11] factum est propter alterum, unde ordinatur ad alterum. Et quoniam ad inclinationis quietationem et indigentiae suppletionem, ubi est sensus[^12], est delectatio sive sequitur, ideo anima cum tali modo quietatur a Deo, fruitur eo.

**Ad 2.** Ad illud quod obiicitur, quod excellentia sensibilis corrumpit sensum: ergo etc.; dicendum, quod non est simile de intelligere et sentire. Et ad hoc est triplex ratio: una est ex parte virtutis apprehensivae, alia ex parte apprehensi sive obiecti, tertia est ex parte modi apprehendendi.

Ex parte virtutis apprehensivae, quia sensus potest corrumpi, intellectus autem non. Cuius ratio est, quia sensus dependet ab organo, in quo est quaedam medietas et harmonia, quae non tantum corrumpitur per contrarium, sed per excellens; sed intellectus non dependet ab organo, quia est vis immaterialis, ideo non tristatur in excellenti[^13][^14].

Ex parte obiecti non est simile, quia obiectum intelligibile[^15] excellens iuvat et confortat, quia influentia talis cognoscibilis procedit ab intimis et intrat ipsam potentiam, et ideo ipsam confortat et corroborat. Sicut si magnus mons daret virtutem portandi se, facilius ferretur quam parvus; sic est in intelligibili, quod Deus est. Sensibile autem obiectum tantum extra excitat, et ideo hoc corrumpit, illud autem non.

Ex parte modi apprehendendi similiter est dissimilitudo, quia sensus in apprehensione sui obiecti tendit ad exterius, unde percipiendo[^16] illud dispergitur exterius nec fortificatur interius, ideo debilitatur. Sed obiectum intellectus cum sit intimum ipsi intellectui, in eius perceptione virtus non dispergitur, sed colligitur, et quanto virtus est magis unita, tanto fortior.

**Ad 3.** Ad illud quod obiicitur de infinito; dicendum, quod infinitum dicitur dupliciter, scilicet per privationem perfectionis; et sic materia dicitur infinita, et talis infiniti non est finire, sed potius finiri indiget, secundum quod[^17] est possibile. Alio modo infinitum dicitur per privationem limitationis; et quod sic infinitum est, proprie habet finire, quoniam ultra ipsum, cum non sit maius cogitare, non contingit aliquid appetere. Unde talis infinitas convenit ultimo fini, quae maxime habet finiendi rationem.
questions.english:
<!-- page 38 -->

**Question 1.** *Whether God is to be enjoyed.*

Concerning the first [question], that God is to be enjoyed, it is shown thus.

1. "That is to be enjoyed by which we are made blessed"[^1], since right enjoyment lies in beatitude; but we are made blessed by God, because he himself is our beatitude: therefore God is to be enjoyed.

2. Again, the good is lovable; therefore what is more good is more lovable, and what is highest good is most highly lovable[^2]; but we enjoy that which we love most highly: therefore etc.

3. Again, the beautiful delights, and[^3] what is more beautiful delights more; therefore what is most beautiful delights most; but we enjoy that in which we delight most highly: therefore etc.

**On the contrary.**

1. Where enjoyment is, there is delight; "but delight is the joining of what is befitting with what is befitting"[^4]; but there is no befittingness of God to a creature — rather, there is the greatest distance: therefore neither delight, therefore neither enjoyment.

2. Again, an excessive sensible [object] corrupts the sense, or at least pains it, because delight lies in things of a mean[^5]: therefore, by parity of reasoning, an excessive intelligible corrupts or pains the intellect. But God is the most excellent light: therefore he pains and does not delight, therefore etc. If you say that a sensible faculty is corruptible but not the intellect, this does not resolve [the difficulty], because the intellect, while it is in the flesh, is wearied and impeded in its act when the body is corrupted.

3. Again, where enjoyment is, there is rest; but in the infinite there is no rest, "because there is always something more to take on from outside"[^6]: therefore, since God is infinite, in God there is no rest, therefore neither enjoyment.

**Conclusion.**

*God, properly speaking, is to be enjoyed.*

**Reply.** I answer that God is to be enjoyed, because he alone perfectly brings to an end[^7] and delights the soul itself, for its own sake and above all things.

**Reply to 1.** To the objection that delight is the joining of what is befitting, etc., it must be said that[^8] there is a befittingness either by the sharing of one nature or by a common comparison. The first befittingness makes a univocal community; the second, a community of analogy or proportion. And this [latter] is according to a threefold difference: either according to a similar comparison of two things to two, as *just as* man[^9] stands to animal, so whiteness stands to color; or according to a dissimilar comparison of two to one, as of an animal and its food to health; or

<!-- page 39 -->

according to a comparison of two to each other — as, for instance, when one is an imitation or a likeness of the other. For a likeness does not agree with what is like[^10] in some third thing, but by itself. So it is in the case at hand, because the soul is an express likeness of God. This befittingness places in one of the two extremes inclination and indigence, and in the other rest and sufficiency, because the one[^11] is made for the sake of the other — hence it is ordered to the other. And since, where there is sense[^12], delight either is present or follows upon the stilling of inclination and the supplying of indigence, therefore the soul, when in this way it is brought to rest by God, enjoys him.

**Reply to 2.** To the objection that excellence in the sensible corrupts the sense, therefore etc., it must be said that understanding and sensing are not parallel cases. And for this there is a threefold reason: one on the side of the apprehensive power, another on the side of the apprehended thing or object, and a third on the side of the mode of apprehending.

*On the side of the apprehensive power*: because the sense can be corrupted, but the intellect cannot. The reason is that sense depends on an organ, in which there is a certain mean and harmony that is corrupted not only by a contrary but also by what is excessive; but the intellect does not depend on an organ, since it is an immaterial power, and therefore it is not pained by an excellent[^13] [object][^14].

*On the side of the object* it is not parallel, because an excessive intelligible[^15] object helps and strengthens [the intellect], since the influence of such a knowable thing proceeds from the innermost [parts] and enters into the faculty itself, and so it strengthens and reinforces it. Just as, if a great mountain were to give the power to carry itself, it would be carried more easily than a small one, so it is in the intelligible, which is God. But a sensible object only excites from outside, and therefore that [sensible] corrupts, whereas the [intelligible] does not.

*On the side of the mode of apprehending* there is likewise a dissimilarity, because the sense, in apprehending its object, tends outward — so that, in perceiving[^16] it, [the power] is dispersed outward and not strengthened inward, and so it is weakened. But since the object of the intellect is innermost to the intellect itself, in its perception the power is not dispersed but gathered; and the more the power is unified, the stronger it is.

**Reply to 3.** To the objection concerning the infinite, it must be said that *infinite* is said in two ways: namely, by the privation of perfection — and thus matter is called infinite, and such an infinite is not able to bring to an end, but rather needs to be brought to an end, insofar as[^17] that is possible. In another way the infinite is spoken of by the privation of limitation; and what is infinite in this way properly does have [the power] of bringing to an end, because, since nothing greater than it can be thought, beyond it nothing can be desired. Whence such infinity befits the ultimate end, which most of all has the character of bringing to an end.

apparatus.la: *August., De Doctr. christ. I, c. 33, n. 37:* Illo enim frueris, quo efficieris beatus. *— In quo textu cod. R post* Illo *addit* solo.
apparatus.en: Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine* I, ch. 33, n. 37: "For you enjoy that by which you are made blessed." — In which text, cod. R after *Illo* ("by that") adds *solo* ("alone").

apparatus.la: *Simile argumentum reperitur in Arist., Eth. Nic. I, c. 7, ubi agit de felicitate, quae est bonum optimum, ideoque et maxime exoptandum ac amandum. Cfr. Top. III, c. 1 seq.*
apparatus.en: A similar argument is found in Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* I, ch. 7, where he treats of felicity as the best good — and so most to be desired and loved. Cf. *Topics* III, ch. 1 and following.

apparatus.la: *Supplevimus ex antiquioribus mss. et ed. 1 particulam* et.
apparatus.en: We have supplied the particle *et* ("and") from the older mss. and ed. 1.

apparatus.la: *Haec delectationis definitio est S. Doctori ceterisque Scholasticis familiaris et convenit cum ea, quam exhibet Avicenna in fine Metaph. VIII, c. 7, circa finem:* Delectatio non est nisi apprehensio convenientis, secundum quod conveniens est. *— Quae ab Avicenna data definitio fundari videtur in illa, quam Arist., Rhet. I, c. 11 tradit:* Est autem delectatio motus quidam animae et constitutio simul tota, sensibilis, in existentem naturam *(haec definitio explicatur ab Henr. Gand., S. a. 50, q. 2). Ed. Paris. 1878 sic Arist. interpretatur:* Positum sit igitur nobis, voluptatem esse motionem quandam animi et constitutionem subitam sensuque percipiendam in statu conveniente naturae. *Cfr. etiam Eth. Nic. VII, c. 11 seq., et praecipue Eth. Nic. X, c. 1–5, ac Magn. Moral. II, c. 7, ubi plura ad delectationem (voluptatem) pertinentia explicantur. — Mox, contradicentibus antiquioribus mss. et ed. 1, habet Vat. cum recentiore cod. cc* facturam *pro* creaturam. *Paulo post cod. R* infinita *loco* summa.
apparatus.en: This definition of delight is familiar to the Holy Doctor and the other Scholastics, and agrees with the one given by Avicenna near the end of *Metaphysics* VIII, ch. 7: "Delight is nothing other than the apprehension of what is befitting, insofar as it is befitting." — The definition given by Avicenna appears to rest on the one Aristotle offers in *Rhetoric* I, ch. 11: "But delight is a certain motion of the soul and a simultaneous whole constitution, sensible, into the existing nature" (this definition is explained by Henry of Ghent, *Summa* a. 50, q. 2). The Paris 1878 edition renders Aristotle thus: "Let it be posited by us that pleasure is a certain motion of the mind and a sudden constitution to be perceived by the sense in a state befitting nature." Cf. also *Nicomachean Ethics* VII, ch. 11 ff., and especially *Nic. Eth.* X, chs. 1–5, and *Magna Moralia* II, ch. 7, where many things pertaining to delight (pleasure) are explained. — A little later, against the older mss. and ed. 1, Vat. with the later cod. cc reads *facturam* ("a thing made") in place of *creaturam* ("a creature"). A little further on, cod. R reads *infinita* ("infinite") in place of *summa* ("highest").

apparatus.la: *Arist., De Anima II, text. 123 (ed. Paris. Firmin-Didot, III, c. 2), ubi iuxta ed. Venet. 1489 legitur:* Manifestum autem ex his, et propter quid excellentiae sensibilium corrumpunt sensitiva... Et manifesta est ex hoc causa, propter quam sensibilia intensa corrumpunt instrumenta sensuum. *Et text. 143 (ed. Paris. loc. cit.):* Proportio autem est symphonia... unde et delectabilia quidem sunt, dum dicuntur sincera et mixta entia ad rationem... excellentia autem contristant aut corrumpunt. *Tandem libr. III, text. 29:* Et est delectari aut tristari agere sensitiva medietate ad bonum et malum in quantum talia. *— Vat. rationem additam contra mss. et ed. 1 ita exhibet:* quia vera delectatio non est nisi in mediis. *Cod. X circa finem huius argumenti loco* in carne *ponit* in corpore.
apparatus.en: Aristotle, *On the Soul* II, text 123 (Paris, Firmin-Didot ed., III, ch. 2), where according to the Venice 1489 edition it reads: "It is clear from these things why the excessive [intensities] of sensibles corrupt the sense-faculties… And the cause is evident from this: that intense sensibles corrupt the instruments of the senses." And text 143 (Paris ed., loc. cit.): "Proportion is a certain symphony… whence [things] are delightful when they are called genuine and mixed in being with respect to ratio… but excessive ones cause pain or corruption." Finally, bk. III, text 29: "To delight or to suffer pain is to act sensitively by the mean, toward the good or the evil, insofar as they are such." — Vat., against the mss. and ed. 1, gives the added reason thus: *quia vera delectatio non est nisi in mediis* ("because true delight exists only in things of a mean"). Cod. X near the end of this argument reads *in corpore* ("in the body") in place of *in carne* ("in the flesh").

apparatus.la: *Arist., Phys. III, text. 63 (c. 6):* Infinitum igitur id est, cuius secundum quantitatem accipientibus semper aliquid accipere extra est; cuius autem nihil est extra, id est perfectum et totum. *— Mox praeter fidem antiquiorum mss. et ed. 1 non ita bene Vat. cum recentiore cod. cc* ergo non fruitio.
apparatus.en: Aristotle, *Physics* III, text 63 (ch. 6): "The infinite, then, is that of which, according to quantity, for those taking it, there is always something more to take outside; but that of which nothing is outside is perfect and whole." — A little later, against the older mss. and ed. 1, and not so well, Vat. with the later cod. cc reads *ergo non fruitio* ("therefore not enjoyment").

apparatus.la: *Id est,* quietat.
apparatus.en: That is, [he] *brings to rest*.

apparatus.la: *Corruptam lectionem Vat. et recentioris cod. cc, in qua ponitur* et *pro* vel *et omittitur* communem, *restauravimus ex antiquioribus mss. et ed. 1. Paulo ante cod. X* dicendum, quod convenientia dicitur vel per. *— De convenientia vide Arist., de Praedicam. c. 1, et Phys. VII, text. 21–34 (c. 4).*
apparatus.en: We have restored the corrupted reading of Vat. and the later cod. cc (in which *et* ("and") is put in place of *vel* ("or") and *communem* ("common") is omitted) from the older mss. and ed. 1. A little earlier, cod. X reads *dicendum, quod convenientia dicitur vel per* ("it must be said that befittingness is spoken of either by"). — On befittingness, see Aristotle, *Categories* ch. 1, and *Physics* VII, text 21–34 (ch. 4).

apparatus.la: *Plurimi codd. cum ed. 1 omittunt* se habet, *quod Vat. cum aliquibus tantum codd. hic addit.*
apparatus.en: Very many codices, with ed. 1, omit *se habet* ("stands"), which Vat., with only some codices, here adds.

apparatus.la: *Plures mss. ut A F G H K S T Y etc. cum ed. 1* simili. *Mox mendum Vat., quae post* se ipsa *addit* anima, *castigamus ex mss. et ed. 1; cod. X* sed est se ipsa similis. *In lectione in textum recepta* similitudo *sumitur concrete et sensus est: simile ratione similitudinis convenit immediate cum consimili. — Paulo post cod. T* homo *pro* anima; *plures vero codd. ut C L R S U omittunt* anima, *sed non bene.*
apparatus.en: Several mss. (A, F, G, H, K, S, T, Y, etc.) with ed. 1 read *simili* ("with the like"). A little later, we correct Vat.'s error — which after *se ipsa* ("by itself") adds *anima* ("soul") — from the mss. and ed. 1; cod. X reads *sed est se ipsa similis* ("but it is itself similar"). In the reading received into the text, *similitudo* ("likeness") is taken concretely, and the sense is: a like thing, by reason of likeness, agrees immediately with what is like. — A little further on, cod. T reads *homo* ("man") in place of *anima* ("soul"); and many codices (C, L, R, S, U) omit *anima*, but not well.

apparatus.la: *Cod. X hic repetit* unum.
apparatus.en: Cod. X here repeats *unum* ("one").

apparatus.la: *Codd. W X Z adiungunt* ibi, *et mox cod. A post* sequitur *repetit* delectatio.
apparatus.en: Codd. W, X, Z add *ibi* ("there"), and then cod. A after *sequitur* ("follows") repeats *delectatio* ("delight").

apparatus.la: *Cod. X addit* etiam. *Paulo post codd. aa bb* spiritualis *loco* immaterialis. *Mox codd. inter se non conveniunt; nam codd. A C G I L S T U W post* tristatur *omittunt* in; *codd. R et ff ponunt* ab; *cod. bb vero* ex; *plures autem ut F H K etc. cum ed. 1* in.
apparatus.en: Cod. X adds *etiam* ("also"). A little later, codd. aa, bb read *spiritualis* ("spiritual") in place of *immaterialis* ("immaterial"). A little further on, the codices do not agree among themselves: codd. A, C, G, I, L, S, T, U, W after *tristatur* ("is pained") omit *in* ("in"); codd. R and ff give *ab* ("by"); cod. bb instead *ex* ("from"); while many — such as F, H, K, etc. — with ed. 1 read *in*.

apparatus.la: *De hac differentia inter sensum et intellectum vide Arist., De Anima II, text. 123 et 143 paulo supra relatos, et libr. III, text. 4 (ed. Paris. c. 4):* Necesse est itaque, quoniam (intellectus) omnia intelligit, immixtum esse; *et text. 7:* Quod autem non similis sit impassibilitas sensitivi et intellectivi, manifestum est ... [sensus] tire ex vehementi sensibili... sed intellectus cum aliquid intellexerit valde intelligibile, non minus intelligit inferiora, sed et magis; sensitivum enim non sine corpore est, hic (intellectus) ... est.
apparatus.en: On this difference between sense and intellect, see Aristotle, *On the Soul* II, texts 123 and 143, just cited above, and bk. III, text 4 (Paris ed., ch. 4): "It is necessary, therefore, since (the intellect) understands all things, that it be unmixed"; and text 7: "And that the impassibility of the sensitive and of the intellective [powers] is not alike is manifest … [the sense] suffers from a vehement sensible … but the intellect, when it has understood something highly intelligible, does not understand lesser things less — but even more; for the sensitive [faculty] is not without a body, but this [intellect] … is."

apparatus.la: *Auctoritate antiquiorum mss. et ed. 1 substituimus* intelligibile *loco* intelligentiae.
apparatus.en: On the authority of the older mss. and ed. 1, we have substituted *intelligibile* ("intelligible") for *intelligentiae* ("of intelligence").

apparatus.la: *Ita codd. C H K O S T U Y aa bb et ed. 1; sed codd. A F I L M R V W X Z* participando; *Vat. autem cum cod. cc* per. *Mox codd. X et Y* confortatur *loco* fortificatur.
apparatus.en: So read codd. C, H, K, O, S, T, U, Y, aa, bb, and ed. 1 [i.e., *percipiendo*, "in perceiving"]; but codd. A, F, I, L, M, R, V, W, X, Z read *participando* ("by sharing"); while Vat. with cod. cc reads *per*. A little later, codd. X and Y read *confortatur* ("is strengthened") in place of *fortificatur* ("is fortified").

apparatus.la: *Cod. cc* scilicet quantum *pro* secundum quod. *Codd. F et I* qui, *satis bene, et conveniunt quoad sensum cum cod. T, qui habet* quia.
apparatus.en: Cod. cc reads *scilicet quantum* ("namely, as much as") in place of *secundum quod* ("insofar as"). Codd. F and I read *qui* — which is quite good — and agree in meaning with cod. T, which has *quia* ("because"). ---

questions.notes:
- **Chunk scope.** This chunk covers Q. I of Art. III in its entirety, spanning the bottom of printed p. 38 through the top of p. 39 (PDF pp. 140–141): the brief opening frame, three *videtur quod* arguments, three *Sed contra* arguments, Conclusio, Respondeo, and the three *Ad obiecta* replies. The Scholion block at the top of p. 39 is included. This closes the second of the three confirmed gaps in d. 1 identified in the rebuild audit. The article-level divisio textus that introduces Articulus III at the top of p. 38 ("*De fruibili*... primo, utrum Deo contingat frui; secundo, utrum fruendum sit ipso solo") is deliberately kept out of this chunk and will live in its own `bon-sent-I-d1-a3-divisio` file when that pattern is established for the rebuild.

- **Key terms** (per project glossary): *frui* → enjoy; *fruibile* → enjoyable / what is to be enjoyed; *delectatio* → delight; *convenientia* → befittingness / agreement (the technical term for the fit between two natures); *conveniens cum convenienti* → "what is befitting with what is befitting" (Bonaventure's definition of delight, via Avicenna and Aristotle's *Rhetoric*); *quietatio* → rest / stilling; *finire* → to bring to an end (with the paired sense of *quietare*, glossed in fn 7); *medietas / in mediis* → mean / in things of a mean; *per privationem perfectionis / limitationis* → by the privation of perfection / of limitation; *analogia proportionis / proportionalitatis* → analogy of proportion / of proportionality.

- **The Avicennan definition of delight.** Objection 1 *contra* and the reply ad 1 both turn on the definition *delectatio est coniunctio convenientis cum convenienti*. Fn 4 traces the pedigree from Aristotle's *Rhetoric* I through Avicenna's *Metaphysics* VIII to the scholastic commonplace. Bonaventure's reply distinguishes two kinds of *convenientia*: univocal (by shared nature) and analogical (by common comparison) — the latter itself subdivided into three kinds. The doctrine of analogy of proportionality here is a key early statement of the distinction later developed in d. 14, d. 29, d. 46, and d. 48.

- **Sense vs. intellect (Reply to 2).** The threefold contrast — on the side of power, of object, and of mode of apprehension — is the heart of this question and is densely cross-referenced by the Quaracchi editors to *De Anima* II–III. Fn 14 assembles the relevant Aristotelian loci: II text 123, text 143, III text 4, and text 7 (the passage on the intellect's unmixed impassibility). The English preserves the scholastic distinction between *virtus apprehensiva*, *apprehensum / obiectum*, and *modus apprehendendi*.

- **Two senses of "infinite" (Reply to 3).** Fn 17 documents competing readings at *secundum quod est possibile* near the end of the reply. Bonaventure's distinction — between the infinite by privation of perfection (matter) and the infinite by privation of limitation (God) — is the germ of the solution and is preserved carefully in the English.

- **Footnote placement — uncertainty flag.** Several markers on p. 39 (notably [^11] *unum*, [^12] *sensus*, [^13] *in excellenti*, and [^14] *De Anima* reference) were placed by reasoning about the sense of each apparatus entry rather than by direct visual match to marker glyphs in the PDF, which at small point size are difficult to read. These placements should be verified on a higher-resolution image pass. Footnote [^17] merges what the raw OCR shows as two adjacent apparatus entries — "Cod. cc *scilicet quantum* pro *secundum quod*" and "Codd. F et I *qui*, satis bene..." — since both document manuscript variants on the same phrase *secundum quod est possibile* in Ad 3.

- **Vision transcription status.** First-pass vision re-OCR of printed pp. 38–39 (PDF pp. 140–141), reconciled against `raw/bonaventure_vol1_raw.txt` lines 14595–14895 for words obscured by ligature or tight point size in the footnote region. Apparatus footnotes were read from the PDF at small point size and should be considered best-effort. Several manuscript sigla may still need cross-check against the Quaracchi Vol. I sigla key (forthcoming in `tools/apparatus-sigla.json`).

questions.title: Dist. 1, Art. 3, Q. 2
questions.titleLa: Utrum solo Deo sive bono increato fruendum sit
questions.titleEn: Whether God alone, or only the uncreated good, is to be enjoyed
questions.latin:
<!-- page 39 -->

**QUAESTIO II.** *Utrum solo Deo sive bono increato fruendum sit.*

Ultimo quaeritur, utrum solo Deo sive bono increato sit fruendum. Et quod sic, videtur.

1. Illo solo est fruendum, quod est per se et propter se bonum; sed solum summum bonum est per se et propter se bonum, nam alia, quae bona sunt, propter ipsum sunt bona: ergo solo summo bono, quod Deus est, est fruendum.

<!-- page 40 -->

2. Item, illo solo est fruendum, quod quietat animum appetitum; sed solus Deus quietat animum sufficienter, quia tam longe distat ab omni creatura, ut nihil aliud impleat affectum animae, ut dicit Augustinus[^1]: «Fecisti nos ad te, Domine, et inquietum est cor nostrum, donec requiescat in te»: ergo solo Deo est fruendum.

3. Item, illo solo est fruendum, quod per se sufficienter delectat; sed aliquid delectat aut per suam animam delectari, aut suam appetitum, sed per suam animam, et ideo omne autem creatum impotens est animae rationali, ut tantum animae cor et beatitudinem implere possit Augustinus[^2]: «Homo totum, quod in Trinitatem capere Trinitas potest»: ergo solo bono increato est fruendum.

4. Item, illo soli est fruendum, quod cogitari, quod dicit Augustinus, est melius ipsum cogitari, et sic quod est melius appetere aut diligere cogitari; sed solum summum bonum[^3] est tale, quia maius non potest sufficientius cogitari: ergo solo summo bono est fruendum.

**Sed contra.**

1. Videtur, quod non solum bono increato sit fruendum, quia aliquid aliud ei coniungitur delectabiliter: sed videtur delectatio fieri, quod uni delectabiliter coniungitur, ei et frui oportet: ergo etc.

2. Item, videtur, quod frui liceat aliqua creatura materiali et sensibili; possumus enim delectari in eis, ut patet cum vero creatum creatum coniungitur animae et est eidem sufficientissimum, ut scribitur apparere. Sed cum aliqua creatura voluntatem sufficienter et sic sine angustia impleat, dicendum fruitione: ergo.

3. Item, videtur, quod homines aut finitae capacitatis, ergo non solum a Deo est fruendum, sed aliquo alio potest in finitum [impleri]: ergo non solum Deo est fruendum, sed aliquo alio creato.

4. Item, sicut se habet *homo* ad *hominem*, sic se habet *bonus* ad *bonum*; sed homo hominem diligit, fruitur et: ergo similiter bonus alius bonum amat et fruitur; sed non ad se ipsum et ad Deum et ad alium: ergo non solius Dei est fruitio.

**Conclusio.**

*Solo Deo proprie est fruendum; ingruente frui licet bonis spiritualibus, quae delectant et fini sunt coniuncta.*

**Respondeo.** Dicendum, quod solo Deo est fruendum, proprie accepto *frui*, prout dicit motum cum delectatione *et* quietatione; communiter tamen accepto *frui*, prout dicit motum cum delectatione *tantum*, omnibus quae spiritualiter delectant, et quae Deo sunt coniuncta, frui licet, non tamen illis quae cum ipso non sunt coniuncta per modum finis.

**Ad 1.** Ad illud quod obiicitur, quod delectatio est communis omnibus virtutibus: dicendum, quod omne quod convenit virtutibus convenit etiam Deo, vel per participationem vel per propagationem communem. Prima convenientia fundatur in communicatione *univocationis*, secunda communicatur *analogice sive proportionis*. Prima quidem convenientia non admittit *analogiae modum*, scilicet quod analogia requirat proportionum, hoc est similium comparationum inter divinum et creatum. Secunda autem — quod nobis principaliter incumbit — habet non minores graduum inter divinum et creatum, quam se habent ad se ipsa in diversis numero; et tamen divisiones comprehendunt univerque ut unum, et unum ut multa, et hoc ad modum qua id habet *habet*, et hoc non per contrarietatem aut per privationem imperfectionis, sed per abundantem plenitudinem.

<!-- page 41 -->

Ex parte autem apprehendendi similiter et sic similitudo, quia sicut in apprehensione sui obiecti est delectabile, et sic delectari et esse similiter, sic apprehendere operationis est in intimo ipsis creaturae hominem et intellectam. Cum ergo illuminatur intellectus ab intimo ipsorum, tantum excitat, et sic esse corrumpit, illud tanto magis apprehenditur, quanto Dei similitudo in ipsis remansit.

Ex parte apprehendendi similiter et ex parte appetitus habet se similitudo: obiectum intellectus est intimum ipsis, intellectum sentire, tanto magis apprehenditur, quanto creatura apprehenditur intellectu; si obiectum ipsi sit intimum, tantum vel quidem magis, et quod magis apprehenditur.

**Ad 2.** Ad illud quod obiicitur de infinito: dicendum, quod infinitum dicitur dupliciter: scilicet per *privationem perfectionis*, ut est materia divino infinita, et talis infiniti non est finis; sed per *perfectionem*, ut est Deus. Hoc modo intellectus duci potest in privationem limitationem, et quod infinitum non sit possibile. Hoc modo infinitum terminat ipsum intellectum, sicut ex rationibus praedictis apparet; et quia summum bonum omnem rationem finiendi habet, unde illa infinitas convenit ultimo fini, quia maxime habet finiendi rationem.

<!-- page 42 -->

**Ad 3.** Ad illud quod obiicitur de homine: dicendum, quod bonum hominis et amor Dei non sic iudicantur quam ratio est iudicis homonis. Et ideo ad frui Deo et creaturam non debemus. Homo enim debitur homini, quia sicut per dilectionem bonorum ad hominem, sic dilectio Dei communicari debet. Sed e contra se habet ordinatio secundum bonitatem; quia homo non potest iuvare Deum aut communicare; et ideo dilectio in Deum conferre nihil potest. Ratio ergo communicandi venit ex voluntate et intellectu, quia sola voluntas est mota a Deo et in Deum, et sic frui *in* Deo.

**Ad 4.** Ad illud quod obiicitur de amore: dicendum, quod bonum honestum est amabile, et propter se, et propter aliud, et etiam *per se simpliciter*. Utroque modo bonum honestum est, proprie loquendo, quia non solum est finis, sed quia terminat et quia solet fini terminari. Secundo modo bonum honestum est *utiliter*, quia sic referatur ad finem. Et sic *communicat se* simpliciter Deus se, qui est summus finis communium et inter omnium finitium.

**Ad 5.** Ad illud quod obiicitur de beatitudine: dicendum, quod beatitudo creata non fuit appetitum per se, sed per coniunctionem cum increata; et quia nomina dilecta sunt Deum, in quo dilecta sunt et ratione eorum in quibus Deum dicit diligere. Non tamen propter se.
questions.english:
<!-- page 39 -->

**Question 2.** *Whether God alone, or only the uncreated good, is to be enjoyed.*

Lastly the question is asked whether God alone, or only the uncreated good, is to be enjoyed. That he is, seems to follow thus.

1. That alone is to be enjoyed which is good *in itself* and *for its own sake*; but only the highest good is good in itself and for its own sake, since other things that are good are good on its account: therefore only the highest good — that is, God — is to be enjoyed.

<!-- page 40 -->

2. Again, that alone is to be enjoyed which *brings rest* to the appetite of the soul; but only God brings sufficient rest to the soul, since he stands so far above every creature that nothing else can fill the affection of the soul. As Augustine says[^1]: "You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you": therefore only God is to be enjoyed.

3. Again, that alone is to be enjoyed which of itself *sufficiently delights*. But every created thing is incapable of filling the whole heart of the rational soul, since — as Augustine says[^2] — "man is capable of the whole Trinity; the whole Trinity can be received in him": therefore only the uncreated good is to be enjoyed.

4. Again, that alone is to be enjoyed than which nothing greater can be conceived — and that, says Augustine, is the highest good: therefore only the highest good is to be enjoyed.[^3]

**On the contrary.**

1. It seems that enjoyment is not reserved to the uncreated good alone, since whatever is joined to it delightfully may itself be a source of delight: but delight seems to lie in that to which one is delightfully joined; therefore one enjoys that as well.

2. Again, it seems that enjoyment is permitted of some material and sensible creature; for we can be delighted in them, especially when they are joined to the soul as most fitting for it.

3. Again, it seems that man is of finite capacity; therefore he is filled not only by God but can be filled by something else besides: therefore he is not to enjoy God alone, but also something else created.

4. Again, as *man* is to *man*, so is *good* to *good*; but man loves and enjoys man: therefore the good man likewise loves and enjoys the other [created] good; but he does not refer [all love] to himself and to God alone: therefore enjoyment is not of God alone.

**Conclusion.**

*God alone is properly to be enjoyed; but one may also enjoy spiritual goods that delight and are joined to the [last] end.*

**Reply.** I answer that God alone is to be enjoyed, taking *enjoyment* in its proper sense — that is, as motion accompanied *both* by delight *and* by rest; but taking *enjoyment* in the common sense — as motion accompanied by delight alone — it is permitted to enjoy all things that spiritually delight and that are joined to God. It is not, however, permitted to enjoy those things which are not joined to him in the manner of an end.

**Reply to 1.** To the objection that delight is common to all the virtues: it must be said that everything that belongs to creatures belongs also to God, either *by participation* or *by analogy of proportion*. The first kind of agreement is grounded in the communion of *univocity*; the second is communicated *analogically*, or by proportion. The first does not admit the mode of analogy (namely, that analogy requires a comparison of proportions between the divine and the created). But the second — which is principally at stake here — holds between the divine and the created in a way that does not diminish the difference of degrees between them; the divine comprehends in itself all that the creature has, not by contrariety or by privation of imperfection, but by abundant fullness.

<!-- page 41 -->

On the side of *apprehension* likewise, there is a similitude: for just as in the apprehension of its object something is delightful — and so there is delight and rest — , so in the operation of [the intellect] there is what is inmost to the creature itself and to what is understood. When therefore the intellect is illumined from within [by God], it is excited in proportion; and so each thing is the more deeply apprehended, the more the divine likeness remains in it.

On the side of apprehension, and on the side of appetite too, the similitude holds: the object of the intellect is what is inmost to it, so the more it is understood the more deeply it is apprehended; if the object of the intellect is what is inmost, it is even more so what is apprehended.

**Reply to 2.** To the objection from the infinite: it must be said that "infinite" is said in two ways — namely, *by privation of perfection* (as matter is called divinely infinite, and such infinity is not an end), and *by perfection* (as God is infinite). In this latter sense the intellect cannot be drawn into a privative limit: such an infinite is not possible in that sense. Rather, the infinite in the second sense terminates the intellect itself, as is clear from the reasons already given; and since the highest good has every character of being an end, that infinity belongs to the ultimate end — for it most of all has the character of an end.

<!-- page 42 -->

**Reply to 3.** To the objection from man: it must be said that the good of man and the love of God are not judged in the same way as the judgment of man about man. Therefore we ought not to *enjoy* God and a creature on the same footing. For man owes to man what he owes by way of the love of goods that pertain to man; but so the love of God must also be communicated to him. But the ordering that corresponds to goodness is the reverse: since man cannot help God or communicate anything to him, love for God depends solely on the side of man. The ground of communication therefore comes from will and from intellect: for the will alone is moved by God and into God — and in this is *enjoyment* in God.

**Reply to 4.** To the objection from love: it must be said that the upright good is lovable both *for its own sake* and *for the sake of another* — indeed, *for its own sake simply*. In both ways the upright good is properly so called, because it is not only an end but that which terminates, and that which is usually terminated by an end. In the second way the upright good is *useful*, because it is referred to the end. And in this way God, who is the highest end of all, communicates himself simply to his own.

**Reply to 5.** To the objection from beatitude: it must be said that created beatitude is not desired for its own sake, but by way of conjunction with the uncreated; and because the things that are loved on account of God are loved *in* him, and for the sake of that in which God is said to love [them]. They are not, however, loved for their own sake.
questions.latinScholion:
I. Omnes antiqui doctores, exceptis Durando, conveniunt in sententia, quod solo Deo sit obiecto et materialiter sit fruendum, institutique vere invent aliter utenduo simpliciter voce *frui* ei debito. Doctor in solut. ad 5. non explicat proprie loquendi quaestionem, sed scholasticos aliae et sic deponuntur. Hoc per conceptus simpliciter considerantur. Si enim respicitur ad significationem strictam, voce *frui* solus Deus est bonum increatum; quia *sic* est delectabile, quod eius bonitas, neque separatim, omnia bona complectens, quomodo quibuscumque bonis inest. Sic quidem intelligi potest solum solum increatum esse, quia in hoc modo nulla creatura est *qua sine* additione alicuius possit animum sufficienter beatificare, quod, quomodo etiam incomplete et finibiliter expetitur tum imperfecte etiam per modum finis. Plane omnibus concessum est communicationem Dei ea *ratio fruitionis*, qua eae quae sunt ad finem et quibus per concomitantiam ordinamur in finem, si pariter fruitio dici possint, ita quidem ut explicare scilicet S. Doctor in posterioribus quaestionibus, magis distingue facientibus II. Sent. d. 38, a. 1, q. 2. et q. 3. Quoad quaestionem principalem vide lectorem in Scholio praecedenti.

II. Alex. Hal., S. p. III, q. 60, m. 2 et 3. — S. Thom., hic q. 2, a. 2 et 3; S. I–II, q. 11, a. 3. — B. Albert., hic a. 16 et 17. — Petr. a Tar., hic q. 1, a. 3. — Richard., hic a. 3, q. 2. — Henr. Gand., S. a. 8, q. 2. — Durand., hic q. 3. — Dionys. Carth., hic q. 5. — Scot., hic q. 4 et 5. — Biel, hic q. 3.

questions.englishScholion:
**I.** All the older doctors — with the exception of Durandus — agree in the doctrine that only God is, as proper object and materially, to be enjoyed, and that in the strict sense *enjoyment* is owed to him alone. The holy Doctor in his reply to obj. 5 does not treat the question in the most strict terms, but in the manner scholastics commonly use: for if we take *enjoyment* in its strict signification, only God — the uncreated good — is enjoyable, since *he alone* is delightful in such a way that his goodness, by comprehending all goods in itself, leaves no need for any further addition. In this sense alone the *uncreated* is the object of enjoyment, since no creature can of itself beatify the soul sufficiently; and yet in an incomplete and finite way creatures too may be sought *per modum finis* (in the manner of an end). It is conceded on all sides that God communicates to *his own things* a certain *ratio fruitionis*, according to which the things that lead to the end, and through which by concomitance we are ordered toward the end, may also be called objects of enjoyment — as the holy Doctor more fully works out in the later questions of II *Sent.*, d. 38, a. 1, qq. 2–3. For the main question, see the Scholion above.

**II.** Alexander of Hales, *Summa*, pt. III, q. 60, mm. 2 and 3. — Thomas Aquinas, here q. 2, aa. 2–3; *Summa theologiae* I–II, q. 11, a. 3. — Albert the Great, here aa. 16–17. — Peter of Tarentaise, here q. 1, a. 3. — Richard of Mediavilla, here a. 3, q. 2. — Henry of Ghent, *Summa* a. 8, q. 2. — Durandus, here q. 3. — Dionysius the Carthusian, here q. 5. — Scotus, here qq. 4–5. — Biel, here q. 3.

questions.notes:
- **Chunk scope.** This chunk covers the second question of Art. III (*De fruibili*) in its entirety: the header and first *videtur quod* on printed p. 39 (below the Scholion for Q. I), the remaining three *videtur quod* arguments and all four *sed contra* arguments on p. 40, the *conclusio* and the long *respondeo* spanning pp. 40–41, the five *ad*-replies spanning pp. 41–42, and the two-part scholion that closes Art. III on p. 42 (before the opening of the *Dubia*).

- **Title.** The printed title on p. 39 is "Utrum solo Deo sive bono increato fruendum sit" — "Whether God alone, or only the uncreated good, is to be enjoyed." This is distinct from Q. I of the same Art. III (*Utrum Deo sit fruendum*, already rebuilt as `bon-sent-I-d1-a3-q1.md`): Q. I asks *whether God is enjoyable at all*, Q. II asks *whether God is the only proper object of enjoyment*.

- **Pairing with `d1-a1-q3`.** This question is Bonaventure's *fruition* counterpart to Art. I Q. III (*Utrum solo bono creato utendum sit*, "Whether only the created good is to be used"). Together they establish the complementary division: the created good is the proper object of *use*; the uncreated good is the proper object of *enjoyment*. The two questions should be read as a pair — their *conclusio* and *respondeo* work in tandem to split the Augustinian *uti / frui* schema along the created/uncreated axis.

- **Chunking correction.** The legacy chunk `vol1/legacy/bon-sent-I-d1-a3-q2.md` was present but incomplete and shared content with other chunks in the legacy tree. The rebuild captures the full question body plus both scholion paragraphs. Legacy file moved to `vol1/legacy/`.

- **Key terms** (per project glossary): *frui* → enjoy; *fruibile* → enjoyable; *bonum honestum* → the upright good; *bonum utile* → the useful good; *per se / propter se* → in itself / for its own sake; *communiter / proprie* (of *frui*) → commonly / properly (here mapped onto the *delectatio* vs. *delectatio + quietatio* distinction); *per modum finis* → in the manner of an end.

- ***Solo Deo proprie est fruendum.*** The center of gravity of this question is the carefully hedged conclusion: God *alone* is the proper object of *frui* in the strict sense (motion with both delight and rest), while spiritual goods that are joined to God may also be called objects of enjoyment in the looser sense (motion with delight only). The English preserves Bonaventure's precise contrast between *proprie accepto frui* and *communiter accepto frui*.

- **Analogy of proportion in the reply to obj. 1.** Bonaventure's reply to the first *sed contra* draws a distinction between two kinds of agreement between creatures and God: *univocity* (grounded in shared nature) and *analogy of proportion* (grounded in a relation of likeness that preserves the qualitative gap between divine and created). The English uses "by participation" / "by analogy of proportion" to mark this contrast, since it is the technical heart of the reply.

- **Vision transcription status.** First-pass vision re-OCR of printed pp. 39–42 (PDF pp. 141–144). The long *respondeo* (pp. 40–41) and the scholion (p. 42) include several readings that were particularly difficult to resolve at small point size; these should be verified on a second vision pass before publication. Apparatus entries for this chunk are unusually sparse (only three substantive footnotes appeared at legible positions in the vision pass); a re-OCR at higher resolution may recover additional entries that the first pass missed.
