questions.notes:
- **Chunk structure**: This chunk covers two questions of D.VIII, Part I, Article I. Q.I concerns whether truth (*veritas*) is a property (*proprietas*) of God's essence; Q.II concerns whether divine being can be thought not to exist (*cogitari non esse*). Both are only partially present — Q.I opens mid-argument, and Q.II breaks off mid-sentence in the *Respondeo*. The initial arguments for Q.I's affirmative side and Q.II's first *pro* argument are lost to OCR gaps.

- **Distinction VIII's structure**: Unlike prior distinctions, D.VIII is divided into two Parts (*Pars I* and *Pars II*), each with its own article. Part I treats the divine attributes of truth, immutability, and simplicity as properties of essence. This is reflected in the chunk ID (*p.1 a.1 q.1*) and will continue across several chunks.

- **Truth's threefold relation (*triplex comparatio*)**: The *Conclusio* of Q.I turns on this schema: truth as indivision of act and potency (relation to subject), truth as representation of supreme unity (relation to principle), truth as ground of discernment (relation to intellect). These three relations track the three transcendental accounts of truth: ontological (*veritas rei*), exemplar (*veritas in ordine ad causam*), and logical (*veritas in ordine ad intellectum*). The second *Conclusio* then adds the key distinction: against *falsity* (privation), truth is found in creatures too; against *admixture* (impurity), it belongs to God alone.

- **"admixture" (*permixtio*)**: The key term of the second *Conclusio*. God's truth is "pure and unmixed" — his indivision has no shadow of potentiality, his imitation no trace of dissimilitude, his expression no obscurity. This is distinct from the Anselmian argument in Q.II and is properly Bonaventure's own analysis.

- **Property without real distinction**: The reply to objection 4 (truth = essence, so neither can be the property of the other) develops a refined account of *proprietas* in God: the third criterion of property in creatures (that the property differs from its subject) is an imperfection arising from non-simplicity, and therefore does not apply to God. What remains is that truth belongs to essence alone (*soli convenit*) and is the ground of knowing it (*ratio innotescendi*) — two marks of perfection without requiring real distinction.

- **Mode of signifying (*modus significandi*)**: The resolution of why truth is the property of essence and not vice versa, even though they signify the same reality: the names retain their distinct *modi significandi* (truth = condition of being; essence = what-it-is) as derived from creaturely usage, and these modes of signification constitute an asymmetric explanatory relation even when the reality signified is identical. This is a careful piece of semantic theology.

- **Q.II — the Anselmian argument**: Arguments 1–7 for the affirmative all derive from variations of the Anselmian ontological intuition: that the first truth is self-confirming in every cognitive act. Arguments 5–7 are particularly sharp: every assertoric utterance, whether affirmative or negative, implicitly posits the first truth. The *sed contra* deploys empirical counter-instances (the fool of Psalm 13, the idolater) and logical objections.

- **"whether it exists / what it is" (*si est / quid est*)**: The standard distinction in scholastic epistemology between existence-cognition and essence-cognition. Bonaventure's resolution turns on the claim — via Hugh of St. Victor — that while the *quid est* of God is inaccessible to the human intellect, the *si est* (the bare fact of his existence) is naturally and indelibly known. Errors about God are always errors of the *quid est* kind, and these only *consequentially* involve denial of existence.

- **OCR**: Argument numbering is somewhat irregular in the OCR (the second argument for the affirmative is labeled "2" twice). The truncation at line 396 (Anselm *contra*—) leaves the *Respondeo* incomplete; the passage on defect of evidence (*defectus evidentiae*) and the full conclusion of Q.II will be in the next chunk. The scholion apparatus at lines 154–227 has been omitted.

DIST. VIII, PART I, ARTICLE I, QUESTION II.

---

*[Continuation of the Respondeo of Question II, begun in the preceding chunk:]*

Not only by reason of a defect of presence can something be thought not to exist, but also by reason of a defect of evidence — because it is not evident in itself, or not evident in the way of proof. But the truth of divine being is evident both in itself and in the way of proof. In itself, because just as we know principles insofar as we know the terms, and because the cause of the predicate is contained in the subject and therefore they are self-evident; so likewise in the matter at hand. For God or the highest truth is being itself, than which nothing better can be conceived: therefore it cannot not exist, nor can it be thought not to exist. For the predicate is contained in the subject. Nor does it have evidence only from itself, but also from proof, since every created truth and nature proves and concludes divine being: because if something is a being by participation and from another, then there is a being by essence and not from another. Every right understanding also proves and concludes it, because the cognition of God is impressed on every soul, and every cognition is through him. Every affirmative proposition likewise proves and concludes it; for every such proposition posits something; and with something posited, the true is posited; and with the true posited, truth is posited, which is the cause of every true thing. A negative proposition, however, does not conclude it except sophistically, as they say. Hence from the fact that nothing exists, or that no truth exists, it does not follow nor can it be inferred that truth exists. For the proposition "nothing exists" destroys every truth. And therefore no affirmation follows from it, and the following is false: "if nothing exists, it is true that nothing exists." And if it be said that every proposition implies its own content, this is true — but if nothing exists, there is no proposition and there is nothing. Augustine, moreover, does not make that argument by way of endorsing it, but by way of inquiry.

It must therefore be conceded that the truth of divine being is so great that it cannot with assent be thought not to exist, except by reason of the ignorance of the one thinking, who does not know what is meant by the name of God. And the arguments for this conclusion are to be conceded, although some of them are sophistical.

1. To the objection on the contrary side, from "the pernicious malice has so prevailed, etc.": it must be said that Damascene is speaking of a thinking that arises from blindness, which is evident from the very word he uses, namely "malice."

2. Similarly, to the objection concerning the idol: it must be said that the idolater errs because he does not know what God is; hence he does not think that God does not exist in the universal sense.

3. To the objection that, with God understood not to exist, other things can still be understood: it must be said that Boethius is speaking of an understanding by which we think something *per impossibile*, but without assenting to it.

4. To the objection that God most escapes our grasp: the response is clear, because what most escapes our grasp is *what he is*, but *that he is* is most evident.

5. questions.notes:
- **Chunk structure**: This chunk completes Q.II of D.VIII P.I A.I (on whether divine being can be thought not to exist), then transitions to Article II (on immutability), opening Q.I of Article II. The chunk breaks off at the beginning of Richard's argument (argument 4 of the *fundamenta* for Q.I of Article II).

- **Defect of evidence — self-evidence (*per se nota*)**: The completion of the *Respondeo* from the prior chunk argues that divine being is immune to both kinds of defect on the side of the knowable: defect of presence (already treated) and defect of evidence. The self-evidence argument mirrors the structure of Anselm's *Proslogion* 2: the predicate (existence, or more precisely, *non posse non esse*) is contained in the subject (the highest truth, being itself). This is Bonaventure's version of what would later be called the ontological argument, but framed epistemically rather than purely ontologically.

- **Negative propositions and Augustine's argument**: Bonaventure sharply qualifies the argument from Q.I argument 7 (Augustine's *Soliloquies* proof that "no truth exists" is self-refuting). He clarifies that Augustine was using it dialectically (*inquirendo*), not endorsing it as a demonstration. The proposition "nothing exists" is not self-refuting in the strong sense — it simply destroys all truth, including itself, and therefore yields no positive conclusion. This is a careful piece of logical analysis.

- **"exterior utterance vs. interior assent" (*exterius / interius*)**: The resolution of the final *sed contra* (argument 6) draws on the Aristotelian distinction from *Posterior Analytics* I.10: one can verbally contradict first principles (*exterius*) without being able to genuinely assent to their negation (*interius*). Bonaventure applies this to the proposition "God does not exist": it can be *expressed* but not genuinely *assented to* by a mind properly exercising reason.

- **Article II opens**: The transition to Article II on immutability follows immediately after the Q.II scholion. The four opening arguments follow the standard scholastic taxonomy of change: (1) substantial change — excluded because God is incorruptible; (2) accidental change — excluded because God has no accidents; (3) act/potency change — excluded because God is pure act; (4) Richard of St. Victor's argument (incomplete). The *Conclusio* will establish immutability as both a fact about God and a divine property.

- **"pure act" (*purus actus*)**: The Aristotelian-Thomistic formula here appears in Bonaventure's own argument, showing his use of the *actus purus* concept as common scholastic currency at this period, though Bonaventure will integrate it within his distinctive emphasis on divine self-sufficiency and the *fontalis plenitudo*.

- **OCR**: The chunk opens mid-*Respondeo* (continuing from the prior chunk's truncation at the Anselm reference). The scholion material (lines covering the Quaracchi editors' discussion of the relationship to the *an Deum esse sit per se notum* question) has been omitted. The chunk ends at the opening words of Richard's argument, which will be completed in the next chunk.

4, 5, 6. To the objection concerning incorruptibility: it must be said, as has been touched on above, that this belongs to creatures; for some creatures are so simple and so united by a good conjunction that no contrariety falls in them, and there is in them no greater ground of corruption than there is in the primary principles. Hence just as the primary principles cannot be resolved into anything, yet they would lapse into nothing if left to themselves; so is it to be understood with respect to certain substances. Hence it is not to be said as simply true that every composite is actually resolvable; but as Anselm says, "it is resolvable either in reality or in understanding." Hence the arguments adduced for this are to be conceded.

7, 8. To the objections concerning mutability (*vertibilitas*): it must be said that every creature is mutable by nature if left to itself.

If the cause of this is asked, it must be said that for this mutability — since it is a pure defect — no efficient or reducing cause leading to non-being is to be assigned, but only a deficient cause. For this reason it must be noted that "nature" is said to be natural origin. Now the origin of a creature is both from nothing and from its own principles: accordingly, something is said to be natural to a creature in two ways — either because it belongs to it from the fact that it is from nothing, or because it belongs to it from the fact that it is from its own principles. And because nothing is not any thing's efficient cause but only its deficient cause, therefore the properties that belong to a creature by reason of its being from nothing are not positive determinations but defects, and are not from a power but from the deficiency of power, and have no efficient cause but only a deficient cause. Such are vanity, instability, and mutability. If therefore it is asked from what source a creature is mutable, I say: not from any efficient cause, but through a deficiency in itself. But according to the sense in which "natural" means what belongs to a thing through its own proper and intrinsic principles, privations and defects are not said to belong to it naturally, but only capacities; and therefore in this sense of "natural," no creature is naturally mutable into non-being — yet it is not said to be naturally immutable either, because "natural" refers to what a thing's nature can bring about; but the principles of a thing are not capable of conserving the thing or of conserving themselves; and therefore immutability is not natural in this sense. Yet neither is it contrary to nature — on the contrary, it is consonant with nature; because every nature desires to be preserved, although it cannot be so of itself, and most especially that creature which desires to be beatified, namely that which is made to the image of God. And because the desire of nature is not in vain where nature falls short, the gratuitous inflow of God supplies what is lacking. And thus it is clear that mutability belongs by nature, but immutability belongs by grace.

9. To the objection concerning the comparison of grace to nature: it must be understood that grace is called an assistance coming from above, with respect to what is beyond the capacity of nature. This assistance is twofold: either with respect to being simply, or with respect to perfect being.

If with respect to being simply — for instance, with respect to the conservation of being, since no primary principles can, being as they are vain things, conserve themselves of themselves — then it does not operate through any infused or given habit. Because it regards being, and because being is common to all things, this grace is common to all. Hence this is grace having the mode of nature, and this is the grace by which the rest of things are said to be immutable.

In the other way, grace is called an assistance with respect to perfect being, and since the perfection of being belongs to those things ordered toward beatitude, it regards well-being and does not belong to all things. Therefore this is a special habit of some, not of all, and this is grace in the mode of grace properly speaking. From these considerations what is objected regarding grace is clear: for the objection proceeds according to grace understood as a special habit distinguished against nature, because in that sense it denotes something newly created; but grace in the sense just described does not.

10. And from this the final objection is also answered: because grace is called an assistance with respect to what is beyond the capacity of nature; and because the conservation of the primary principles is beyond the capacity of nature, while the going-forth of operations is not — indeed, it is below it — therefore the matter is clear, etc.

questions.notes:
- **Chunk structure**: This chunk contains only the replies to objections (numbered 4–10) for Q.II of D.VIII P.I A.II. The question itself, the arguments, and the *Respondeo* proper are entirely absent from this OCR section, which opens mid-discussion. The subject matter — from context and the replies — is whether immutability is a *property* of God alone (*proprium Dei*), i.e., whether any creature can be said to be immutable. The replies defend the claim that immutability in the strict sense belongs to God alone, while conceding a weaker immutability to some creatures by grace.

- **Missing chunk**: A full chunk corresponding to D.VIII P.I A.II Q.II's question, arguments, *sed contra*, and *Respondeo* is absent from the OCR sequence. The gap between the previous chunk (which ended at the opening of A.II Q.I's *fundamenta*) and this one is substantial; Q.I's full *Respondeo* and Q.II's entire body are missing. This should be flagged for recovery from the PDF.

- **"mutability" (*vertibilitas*) and "immutability" (*invertibilitas*)**: The central terms. *Vertibilitas* (literally "turnability") is Bonaventure's technical term for the creature's inherent capacity to lapse into non-being or to undergo change; *invertibilitas* for resistance to such lapse. The distinction maps onto the pair *ex nihilo / ex principiis propriis* — what belongs to a creature from its creaturely origin (from nothing) vs. what belongs to it from its own intrinsic constitutive principles.

- **"from nothing as deficient cause"**: A characteristic Bonaventurian metaphysical move. *Ex nihilo* does not imply that nothing is an efficient cause of defects in creatures; rather, nothing is a *deficient cause* — it is the privative ground of instability, vanity, and mutability. These are not posited by God's creative act but reflect the creature's own ontological poverty as something that was not. This is closely related to Bonaventure's teaching on *vestigium* and the creature's intrinsic finitude.

- **Twofold grace (*duplex adiutorium*)**: The reply to objection 9 introduces an important distinction between (1) grace in the mode of nature (*gratia habens modum naturae*) — universal divine conservation, by which all creatures are preserved in being and thus in a secondary sense "immutable"; and (2) grace in the mode of grace properly speaking — the special infused habit ordered toward beatitude, belonging to rational creatures alone. The first corresponds roughly to what later theology calls *concursus* or *conservatio*; the second to *gratia gratum faciens*. This distinction resolves the objection that immutability, if from grace, must be a special and divisible gift rather than universal.

- **"desire of nature is not in vain" (*desiderium naturae non est frustra*)**: A standard axiom of scholastic teleology, here applied to the creature's desire for conservation and beatification. Where natural desire exceeds natural capacity, divine grace supplies the deficit. This grounds the immutability of spiritual creatures in God's gracious sustenance rather than their own ontological resources.

- **"the empyrean by reason of its contents"**: The opening fragment (before the reply to objections 4–6) belongs to a reply to an objection apparently concerning whether the empyrean heaven is immutable or incorruptible by reason of its simplicity or by reason of what it contains (i.e., the blessed). This is characteristic of the cosmological discussion of incorruptibility that likely featured in the missing *Respondeo*.

- **OCR**: This chunk is fragmentary. All content prior to the reply to objections 4–6 is missing, and the preceding chunk (D.VIII P.I A.II Q.I) is also incomplete. The full A.II section should be reconstructed from the PDF before finalization.

In parte ista circa litteram incidit hic ' quaestio

DIVISIO TEXTUS.

Supra egit Magister de proprietatibus , quae
respiciunt essenliam. Hic agit de his, quae respiciunt personas ; el haec pars habet duas partes. Quia
enim distinctio personarum attenditur secundum
duplicem emanationem, scilicet generationis et processionis, ideo primo agit de generatione, secundo
vero de processione, infra distinctione decima :
Nunc vero post Filii aeternitatem de Spiritu sancto etc.

Item, prima pars habet duas partes: in prima
ostendit, quid de generatione Filii est sentiendum,
secundo ex incidenti, quo sermone est ipsa exprimenda , ibi : Hic quaeri potest, cum generatio Filii
a Patre etc.

Prima iterum pars habet quatuor partes '.
Primo proponit veritatem, quae est a catholicis retinenda, scilicet quod generans et genitus sunt per
generationem distincti et coaeterni , ita quod generatio est distinctiva et aeterna. In secunda contra
hoc opponit per oppositionem haereticorum , ibi:

Doctorum Augustini et Ambrosii, ibi: Qui hoc dicit
non intelligit , etiam natum esse etc. In quarta et

ultima respondet , compescendo inquisitionem superfluam haereticorum et etiam catholicorum superbo-
rum, ibi: Sed quaeris a me, inquit Amhrosius,
ubi ostendit quod imperscrutabile ^ est sacramentum
generationis.

ARTICULUS UNICUS.

De generationo in
QUAESTIO I.

Utruni in divinis generatio ponenda sit.

Circa primum, quod generatio sit in divinis,
ostenditur^:

1. Primo a minori. Multo fortius debet esse
generatio in eo qui generationem aliis tribuit, quain
in his quae recipiunt; sed generatio est in creaturis: ergo et in Deo qui tribuit. Et hoc est quod
dicitur Isaiae ultimo^: Si ego generationem aliis
Irihuo , sterilis ero ? dicit Dominus, quasi dicat, non.

2. Item, ostenditur illud idem a. posteriori. Per
prius enim est paternitas in Deo quam in creatura;
sed paternitas et generatio vere est in creatura:
ergo et in Deo. Quod prius sit ibi , dicit Apostolus
ad Ephesios tertio^: Ex quo omnis paternitas in
caelo et in terra nominatur.

3. Item, ostenditur hoc ipsum a simili, quia
omne quod perfectionis est, attribuendum est Deo,
in quo est summa omnis perfectionis ; sed generatio
est perfectionis in creatura, ut vult Philosophus%
quia «perfectum est quod potest generare quale
ipsum est»: ergo etc.

4. Item , illud idem ostenditur alia ratione
sic ^ : divina natura est summe bona et actualissima: ergo summe potest et vult se communicare;
sed prima et summa ratio communicandi est in generatione : ergo necesse est in divinis ponere gene-
rationem.

CoNTRA : 1 . Generatio in creaturis aut est per- m ,
fectionis , aut impe^'fectionis. Si perfectionis , tunc
ergo, cum substantiae spirituales et incorporales
sint nobilissimae , debet in eis generatio esse: ergo
cum non sit in eis , non est nobilitatis ; sed quod non
est nobilitatis non est in Deo: ergo etc.

2. Item , ubi est generatio , ibi est variatio ; generatio enlm est species motus , et inter omnes spe-
cies motus maior est variatio in motu secundmn
substantiam, quia est entis in potentia, minor in
motu secundum locum ' : ergo cum in Deo non sit
variatio nec aliqua species motus, etiam illa quae
minima est, ut loci mutatio: ergo nec generatio.

3. Item, ubi est generatio, ibi est corruptio,
unde Philosophus ' dicit , quod >< propter longe stare
a principio reliquo modo complevit esse Deus, continuam in his faciens generationem » ; et huiusmodi
signum est, quod sola corruptibilia generant et generantur in creaturis; sed in Deo nulla cadit cor-
ruptio: ergo nec generatio.

4. Item, ubi est generatio, ibi est» nutritio;
unde ad tot et plures se extendit vis nutritiva
quam generativa; sed in Deo non est vis nutritiva:
ergo nec generativa, ergo nec nutritio, nec generatio: ergo generatio non est in divinis.

DuB. VIII.

Item quaeritur de hoc quod dicit Hilarius, quod

comprehendimus ; ipse autem' perfecte noyit eam.

DuB. IX.

Item quaeritur de hoc quod dicit: Quod ex vivo

novitate naturae. Videtur enim falsum, quia puer nascitur de patre et matre viventibus, et tamen utrum-
que habet, scihcet imperfectionem et novitatem.

Respondeo: Ratio Hilarii, sicut patet per litteram
sequentem ', intelligenda est de vivo per essentiam;
ubi enim est vivens per essentiam, non fit ex non vivo
vivens, sicut flt in vivente ^dv participationem, ubi
non generatur vivum ex vivo nisi per non vivum,
ut patet, quia homo non generatur ex homine nisi
mediante semine.

DuB. X.

Item quaeritur de hoc quod dicit: Neque ex derivatione, sed ex vi?'tute nativitas est. Videtur contra-
rium , quia secundum Dionysium * et Anselmum Pater
se habet ad Filium et Spiritum sanctum, ut fons, et
illi ut rivi ; sed rivus est a fonte per derivationem.

Respondeo: Dicendum, quod nativitas , quae est
per derivationem , attenditur quantum ad transmutationem aliquam circa illud quod transmutatur, et
ita dicit passionem quandam, ac per hoc infirmitatem^; sed vivens, quod est vita, est actus purus,

DuB. XI.

Ilem quaeritur de hoc quod dicit: Ubi Pater
auctor est, ibi et nativitas est. Videtur quod improprie dicit", quia auctoritas dicit causalitatem; sed
haec non recipitur in divinis: ergo etc.

Respondeo: Dicendum, quod auctoritas dicit
quandam principalitatem sive auctoritatem in persona , quae nihil habet ab alio , sed ab ipso omnes ;
et ista auctoritas in Patre est innascibilitas ; unde non
dicit causalitatem , sed privationem principii , et per

DuB. XII.

Item quaeritur de hoc quod dicit: Quod vero ab
aeterno natum est, id, si 7ion aeternum natum

quod esse Patrem sit proprie proprium illius personae : ergo cum tale semper conveniat , aut aliter res
non habet esse perfectum, sequitur de necessitate:

tamen ratione connotati habet imperfectionem coniunctam, secundum quam non tantum impossibile, sed
etiam non intelligibile est, aliquid ab aeterno creari '^

DuB. XIII.

Item quaeritur de hoc quod dicit: Sed se ipsum
deniutare nascendo; quia secundum hoc, cum Filius
Dei prius esset et postea ex Virgine natus sit ": ergo

aliam \ oportet mutationem fieri in illa natura, sed

DUBIA CIRCA LITTERAM MAGISTRI.

DUB. I.

In parte ista incidunt dubitationes circa litteram,
et primo dubitatur de hoc quod dicitur: Non est
aliud Pater, aliud Filius, aliud Spiritus sanctus,
quamvis personaliter etc. Videtur enim falsum
quod dicitur, quia bene sequitur: Petrus est albus
homo, ergo est animal album, quia idem significat
albus et album : ergo pari ratione , quia idem significat ' alius et aliud, sequitur: esl alius, ergo
est aliud ens. Si tu dieas , quod non esl simile de
hoc nomine alius et de hoc nomine em^; contra:
bene sequitur: est ahus homo, ergo est aliud animal: ergo a simili illud sequitur.

Respondeo : Dicendum , quod quia in Deo est soiuUo i.
singularis alietas, quia alietas est suppositi cum
omnimoda unitate naturae: ideo singulari modo
oportet exprimi. Et quoniam masculinum genus impnrtat quandam distinctionem vel discretionem ° ,
ideo respicit personam; sed neutrum propter indistinctionem respicit naturam: et ideo alius impor-
tat alietalem in persona , aliud '" in natura , et ideo
in divinis non idem significant.

Posset etiam dici, quod in ci'ea'ui'is aliud si-soiuiioa.
gnificat", cum dico: iste est alius ab illo, et aliud,
cum dico: est aliud; et unum sequitur ad aliud.
Non sic in divinis; et non est simile de albo, quia
album imponitur a forma speciali , quae est albedo.

Respondeo: Dicendum, quod nomen significans
subsiantia substantiam in divinis reperitur secundum triplicem
piiciier si- modum. Quoddam enim significat' substantiam et

gnificatur. , , . i ^ ■

per modum substantiae , ut nomen substantivum ,
ut Deus ; et tale nullo modo plurificatur nec dicitur
pluraliter, sive sit substantivum, sive substantivatura; ut^ hoc nomen aeternus; sic accipitur in Sym-
bolo. Quaedam signiticant substantiam per modum
adiacentiae, sicut nomina adiectiva adiective retenta *;
et talia, quia trahunt numerum a substantivis , dicuntur plurahter, et de genere talium sunt verba
et participia. Alia sunt nomina, quae important
substantiam in adiacentia, connotando intra relationem mutuam, qualia sunt coaeterni^ ; et talia ex
duplici causa possunt dici pluraliter, tum ratione
consignificationis sive modi significandi , tum ratione connotationis. Et sic patet, quod nulla est con-
tradictio.

Quod ° autem oblicitur , quod pluralis numerus
plurificat formam; dicendum, quod hoc non est
verum in adiectivis '.

DUB. III.

Sed contra: Si emanatio procedens a Deo est ei
coaeterna, sieut emanatio procedens a creatura est

Respondeo: Dicendum, quod egressus splendoris" a luce vel igne est egressus connaturalis ; el
talis est egressus Filii a Patre, non autem egressus
crealurae a Creatore, immo est voluntarius; et argumentum est bonum in proposito.

Item, si Dei Filius, inquit Augustinus, virtus Ka''o s.
etsapientia. Haec est secunda ratio Augustini: Filius
Dei est virtus et sapientia: ergo si non est aeternus,
aliquando fuit Deus sine virtute et sapientia; sed

In parte ista sunt dubitationes circa litteram ,
et primo de argumento haeretici, quod facit ibi:
Aut nato iani Filio, aut non nato. Videtur enim

' non habent posse in eura. '

DIST. XVI. ART. UNICUS OUAEST. III.

OUAESTIO 111.

Quibus modis facta sil missio visihilis.

Tertio quaeritur, quibus modis fit' missio visibilis. Et accipiuntur diversi modi ex Scripturis. Fi-
lius enim visibiliter apparuit in creatura rationali, ut
in homine; Spiritus vero sanctus in irrationali, ut
puta in columba, igne et flatu. Quaeritur ergo de
diversitate horum modorum apparendi; et videtur,
quod non fuerlnt modi ^ convenientes, hoc modo.

1. Spiritus sanctus est aeque nobilis persona,
• ut Filius : ergo in aeque nobili creatura debet mani-

festari, ut Filius.

2. Item, si Filius propter assumtionem humanitatis sive apparitionem in forma servi est minor
Patre, immo factus minor Angelis^: ergo multo fortius Spiritus sanctus ex apparitione in igne non tan-
tum minor Deo, sed etiam homine; sed hoc nullo
modo congruit: ergo non congruit Spiritui sancto
apparere in creatura irrationali. — Si tu clicas, quod
Filius apparuit in homine assumto et unito, Spiritus
autem sanctus non est columbae unitus vel igni;
contra: unio nihil auferl divinitati: ergo propter
unionem non debet dici minor. Si ergo dicitur minor, hoc est propter apparitionem: ergo etc.

3. Item, videtur quod Spiritus sanctus fuit unitus * , quia Spiritus sanctus apparebat in illa columba,
et non in aUa; et rursus apparebat ipseibi% non
alia persona: ergo alio modo erat in illa quam Pater et Filius, et aliter in illa quam in alia; sed aliter
non potuit esse in illa quam alia persona quantum
ad substantiam nec quantum ad operationem, quia
eadem est substantia et operatio in Trinitate, ergo
quantum ad unionem: ergo etc. — Si tu dicas, quod
apparuit sicut in signo, tunc quaero: aut illud signum fuit a nalura, aut ab insiitutione °. Si a natura,
tunc pari ratione et omnis alia columba; si ab insti-

-tutione, quaeritur: quis instituit?

4. Item, Filius apparuit visibiUter uno modo
tantum et in una creatura; quaeritur, quare non

-similiter Spiritus sanctus? et videtur, quod ita deberet esse, quia sicut in Filio nulla cadit varietas, iramo
omnimoda uniformitas, ita et in Spiritu sancto: ergo
debuit apparere tantum in una specie, ut Filius^.

5. Item, Filius tantum semel apparuit visibiliter,

quia tantum semel est incarnatus, non amplius. Quae- '^jljj^*''",'"ritur ergo, unde hoc est, quod Spiritus sanctus pluries
apparuit, ut puta non tantum semel in igne, sed etiam
quousque dabatur Spiritus sanctus ' ? — Si dicas,
quod illa, in quibus Spiritus sanctus apparuit, statim
esse desierunt post apparitionem , et ideo oportuit
rursum alia fleri; tiinc ergo videtur, quod nec illa AHa dimcuicolumba fuerit vera, nec ignis, cum tam columba
quam ignis habeant' virtutem permanendi; et si hoc
in illa apparitione non fuit, tunc ergo non fuerunt
vera, sed falsa, et non fuerunt apparitiones , sed
praestigia et illusiones, sicut sunt phantasmata daemonum et aliorum magorum.

6. Ultimo quaeritur, quare tot modis apparuit «"""?
Spiritus sanctus , et quare in aha specie in capite '"Sns!"'
quam in membris, ut in Christo et Apostolis ?

Apparitio Filii congruenter facta est semel in una
et rationabili substantia iinita; Spiritus vero
sanctus congruenter apparuit pluries in pluribus et irrationabilibus creaturis ut signis.

Respondeo: Dicendum, quod finis imponit necessitatem his quae sunt ad flnem; ideo modus
apparendi sumendus est iuxta flnem apparitionis.
Apparuit autem Filius in carne, ut esset mediator , Spiritus vero sanctus, ut doctor, loannis de-
cimo sexto'°: Cum venerit, docebit vos omnem ■
veritatem. Ad mediationem autem necessaria est

unitus. Ad eritditionem autem ignorantium intervenit
signum " ; ideo Spiritus sanctus apparuit in creatura conciusio 2.
ut signatum in signo.

Quoniam ergo nihil esi Deo perfecte unibile nisi
beatificabile , et hoc solum est substantia rationalis ;
ideo Filius in sola substantia rationali apparuit.

Quia vero uSui significationis purae '^ convenit

crederetur unita, non tantum significans; ideo Spi-

quia Filius factus est homo passibilis, sed Spiritus
sanctus non est factus columba.

3. .\d illud quod obiicitur, quod est unitus columbae ; dicendum , quod est unio secundum verita.-
tem, et est unio secundum intentioneni^. Primo modo
uniuntur illa quae uniuntur in natura vel persona;
secundo modo uniuntur significatum et signuni; et
hoc modo unita est persona Spiritus sancti illis formis, in quibus apparuit.

Si autem quaeratur, unde veniebat talis unio;
n- dicendum , quod dispositive a proprietatibus creaturae, in quibus nata erat personam Spiritus sancti
declarare °, sicut ftatus spiritum , ignis amorem, columba donum propter fecunditatem. Sed completive

et ideo lam columba t(uam ignis simul cum apparitione etiam incepit et desiit '.

5. Ex hoc patet , quare ° Spiritus sanctus non p.iin..i
tantum semel apparuit, sed pluries, Filius autem
non, quia columba et ignis statim post apparitionem
esse desierunt, non autem homo. — Ex hoc patet
etiam, quod etsi '° columba illa et ignis essent verum Ad di

per redemptionem ; el ila fuit in Christo, et haec est

apparuit in columba, quia '^ erat pretium redemptio-

nis primogenitorum et erat animal integrum et perfectum. Potest etiam esse per vitae influentiam quantum
ad sensum etmotum, et hoc mediantibus Sacramentis; et haec plenitudo est in sacerdotibus, et ideo
datus est eis Spiritus sanctus in specie flatus, loannis
vigesimo'": Insufflavit in eos dicens: Accipite Spiritum sanctum: quorum remiseritis peccata etc.
Potest etiam tertio modo esse per cognitionis administrationem sive doctrinam; et haec plenitudo est
in Apostolis et Doctoribus, et ideo Spiritus sanctus
apparuit eis in linguis igneis ". Ex his patet responsio el sufficientia modorum apparendi et obiectorum.

quia pro et ideo , quibus positis ordo ct connexio

quia. — Cfr. Levit. 12, 6. seqq.

DUB. I.

In parte ista sunt dubitationes circa litteram,
€t primo dubitatur de hoc quod dicit, quod Filius
in quantum missus , icl est factus, niinor est Patre.
Contra quod sic obiicitur: omnis actus, secundum
quem aliquem contingit fieri minorem, est indignitatis. Si ergo Filius ratione missionis est minoratus,
ergo missio pertinet ad indignitatem '. Iteni, quandocumque aliquis de aequali fit minor, mutatur;
sed Filius ante missionem erat aequalis, et modo
est minor: ergo etc.

Respondeo: Dicendum, quod quaedam dicuntur
de Filio Dei per essentiam, quaedam per ^ unionem,
quae tanta fuit, ut faceret hominem Deum et Deum

Dei est ininor: sed hoc dictum est per unionem,

indignitas , nulla mutabilitas in eius persona; et
sic solvitur utrumque obiectum, quia utraque ratio
procedit, intellecto ^ quod secundum eandem naturam
fieret minor, secundum quam erat aequalis, et ita
desineret esse aequalis. Nunc autem simul est minor

DUB. II.

Item quaeritur de hoc quod dicit, quod .se

duae personae, quod non conceditur.

Respondeo: Dicendum, quod verum est, quod
maiorem diversitatem dicunt maior et minor , quia
diversitatem virtutis et naturarum; sed ad hanc^
diversitatem , quamvis sit maior , non sequitur diversitas in persona, quia plures naturae possunt esse
in una persona. Quoniam ergo in Christo cadit diversitas naturarum et ita virtutum , non autem per-
sonaruni: ideo dicitur maior et minor ratione diversarum virtutum , non autem alius et alius, cum
non habeat diversas personas ^

DUB. III.

Item quaeritur de hoc quod dicit, quod minoratus esl paulo 7ninus ab Angelis. Videtur enim
falsum , quia super illud ad Hebraeos secundo ' :

DuB. V.

DUB. I.

In parte isla sunt dubitationes circa litteram,

Item, praedicatum, quod dicitur de tota Trinitate,

Pater est solus Deus.

Respondeo: Dicendum , quod quando solus per

tate, ita quod non de Patre. Sed in illis locutionibus :
soli Deo honor et gloria "^, et consimilibus solus Deus
non accipitur pro unica persona, excludendo alias
personas, sed pro tota Trinitate, excludendo alias
naturas; et Magister ita accipit, ac si Augustinus
vellet dicere', quod hoc, scilicet soliis Deus, praedicaretur de Trinitate, et non de Patre. Sed ipse vult,
quod non proprie dicilur. Et illud manifestum est, si
inspiciatur, qualiter solus debet addi ad praedicatum ^

DUB. II.

dicimus solum Deum, quamvis semper sit cum

Dominus vobiscum dicitur hominibus, non bestiis.

nullus homo; sed dictio exceptiva non excipit
